messages.body_plain:
Sorry, I didn’t compile to check these kinds of
errors.

We haven’t implemented size() for vectors yet.
You’ll need to use cols() or num_elements().

- Bob

> On Jan 30, 2015, at 4:55 PM, Tymoteusz Wołodźko <t.wol...@ibe.edu.pl> wrote:
>
> Thank you both for interesting information and comments.
>
> Cameron Bracken, thanks for the example. It is not that straightforward, so an example is always helpful as a place to start!
>
> Greetings,
> Tim
>
>
> 2015-01-30 19:59 GMT+01:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> Thanks for sharing.
>
> There's a serious problem with the model as written.
> The parameter declaration:
>
> > parameters {
> >   real xi;
>
>
> is not consistent with the model:
>
> >   xi ~ uniform(-.5,.5);
>
> The general rule is that any parameter value matching the constraints
> (which here includes xi = 10, for example), should have support in
> the model.
>
> To fix, you need to declare:
>
>   real<lower=-0.5,upper=0.5> xi;
>
> If you don't, what will happen is that any path leading outside
> of (-0.5,0.5) will cause an immediate rejection and sampling can
> devolve.  You'll also get failed random initializations.
>
> We also don't recommend those very diffuse priors that were
> in the early BUGS models (or the interval constraints they switched
> to later).  There are a few sections in the regression chapter of
> the manual that we've added recently on what we do recommend.  It can
> also be a huge help with computation to have less diffuse priors, even
> if they're not informative enough to have a noticeable impact on the posterior.
>
> Maybe we should add the GEV density as a built-in.
>
> It's possible to speed up the implementation below with
> some algebra by treating y as a vector in the function.
> We'd eke out even more speed with a built-in version and also
> potentially avoid some calculations you don't need.
>
> The implementation below would be faster if you converted
> everything to vectors, but it's not so straightorward to write
> because we don't have a vector version of pow(), so I had
> to define some intermediates to avoid redundant calculations.
> I haven't tried to validate this does the right thing, but
> it'd look something like this:
>
> real gev_log (vector y, real mu, real sigma, real xi) {
>   vector[size(y)] z;
>   vector[size(y) + 1] lp;
>   real inv_xi;
>   real inv_xi_p1;
>   real neg_inv_xi;
>   z <- ((1 + y) - mu) * (xi / sigma);
>   inv_xi <- inv(xi);
>   inv_xi_p1 <- 1 + inv_xi;
>   neg_inv_xi <- -inv_xi;
>   for (n in 1:size(y))
>     lp[n] <-  inv_xi_p1 * log(z[n]) + pow(z[n],neg_inv_xi);
>   lp[size(y) + 1] <- size(y) * log(sigma);
>   return -sum(lp);
> }
>
> and then it's just
>
>   y ~ gev(mu,sigma,xi);
>
> in the model.  This should be quite a bit faster than the
> simpler implementation.  But then it may not be worth the ugliness
> if it's already fast enough.
>
> I may pull this out as an optimization case study for the manual.
>
> - Bob
>
> >     real z;
> >     z <- 1 + (y - mu) * xi / sigma;
> >
> >   }
>
>
> data {p
>   vector[N] y;
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jan 30, 2015, at 1:33 PM, Cameron Bracken <cameron...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Here is the most simple example of an extremes model, fitting a univariate stationary GEV distribution.
> >
> > functions {
> >
> >   real gev_log (real y, real mu, real sigma, real xi){
> >     real z;
> >     z <- 1 + (y - mu) * xi / sigma;
> >     return -log(sigma) - (1 + 1/xi)*log(z) - pow(z,-1/xi);
> >   }
> >
> > }
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=0> N;
> >   real y[N];
> > }
> >
> > transformed data {
> >   real min_y;
> >   real max_y;
> >   min_y <- min(y);
> >   max_y <- max(y);
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real xi;
> >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> >   // location has upper/lower bounds depending on the value of xi
> >   real<lower=if_else( xi < 0, min_y + sigma / xi, negative_infinity() ),
> >        upper=if_else( xi > 0, positive_infinity(), max_y + sigma / xi )> mu;
> > }
> > model {
> >   # priors on component parameters
> >   sigma ~ gamma(.0001,.0001);
> >   #mu ~ uniform
> >   xi ~ uniform(-.5,.5);
> >
> >   for(i in 1:N) {
> >     y[i] ~ gev(mu, sigma, xi);
> >   }
> > }
> >
> > On Friday, January 30, 2015 at 12:48:17 AM UTC-7, Tymoteusz Wołodźko wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> > Actually I must say that I just want to learn more on Bayesian implementations of this kind of models, so I don't have any certain model in mind at this moment, but rather was looking for some working examples. I would be very grateful for some, even the simple "handbook" ones, to get better idea on this.
> >
> > I have already seen this slides for BUGS:
> > http://www.math.helsinki.fi/openbugs/IceBUGS/Presentations/JaggerIceBUGS.pdf
> >
> > but unfortunately I don't find them helpful. I have also seen other authors mentioning Bayesian approach to EVT but rarely going into details.
> >
> > Maybe it would be good to paste a simple example on Stan github page with examples..?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Tim
> >
> >
> >
> > 2015-01-29 20:01 GMT+01:00 Cameron Bracken <cameron...@gmail.com>:
> > I have implemented all sorts of extremes models in stan. Everything from stationary univariate GEV to spatial extremes models. I am happy to discuss if you have anything specific in mind.
> >
> > Cameron
> >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for the help everyone. Applying the "Matt trick" really made things go faster.

After 5,000 iteration some of the R-hat coefficients are still between 1.3-1.4. It might be that I need better initialisation values, though. Right now I am just letting Stan set some at random.

This is the "final" code with priors on the coefficient intercept: https://gist.github.com/demodw/88552f402d82669bfef6

David

Den fredag den 30. januar 2015 kl. 22.22.13 UTC+1 skrev Andrew Gelman:
> Matt trick yes.  But I say no on the <lower=0,upper=10> thing.  I much prefer soft constraints.
>
> > On Jan 30, 2015, at 11:37 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > The real Stan folks can give you a more complete answer, but I noticed a few things that you can change that might help things out:
> >
> > 1. You can get rid of all the uniform(0,10) sampling statements and just declare the parameters with lower=0 and upper=10 constraints. Not sure how much this will help performance, but it certainly won't hurt.
> >
> > 2. You can use the "Matt trick" for all the normal priors on the coefficients. For example, for a0, you would do
> >
> > parameters {
> >   a0_raw ;
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >  a0 ;
> >  a0 <- a0_raw * a0_sigma ;
> > }
> > model {
> >  a0_raw ~ normal(0,1) ;
> > }
> >
> > Making the sampling statements all for standard normals often helps quite a bit.
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, January 30, 2015 at 5:45:14 AM UTC-5, David Westergaard wrote:
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I am trying to develop a model with four nominal variables (age, gender, analysis method, disease type), and the interaction between some of these. The setup is a kind of repeated measures. Some of the participants have been measured 100+ times, other have been measured once. The response value is numerical. On a small dataset the model seems to perform as I would have expected, however on the full data set, with ~400k observations, the model is simply to slow. After 12 hours the model has not even gone through 500 iterations in any of the four chains run in parallel, whereas in the JAGS the roughly equivalent model took just under a day with ~10,000 iterations. I have tried to follow the guidelines for code optimisation in the manual plus what I have found in this forum.

> > > What I would like to model is,
> > >
> > >   y = a0 + a_S + a_age + a_sex + a_sex*age + a_analysis + a_type + a_age*type + a_sex*type + a_age*sex*type

> > > a_S is the coefficient for each subject, modelled in as suggested by Kruschke (2010) for repeated measure experiments. I have precomputed all of the interactions in R, since I could not find a clever way of assigning each coefficient in Stan its own prior without a nested loop.

> > >
> > > https://gist.github.com/demodw/4fe7e274bcbb76c0353a
> > >
> > > Thanks!
> > >
> > > David

messages.body_plain:
My guess is that with so many varying intercepts, you’re running
into identifiability issues:

mu[i] <- a0_raw + aS_raw[subj[i]] + a1_raw[age[i]]
          + a2_raw[sex[i]] +  + a3_raw[analysis[i]] + a4_raw[type[i]]
          + a1a2_raw[sexage[i]] + a1a4_raw[agetype[i]] + a2a4_raw[sextype[i]]
          + a1a2a4_raw[agesextype[i]];

If agesextype is an interaction term, it’ll only make things
worse.

There’s a chapter in the manual on problematic posteriors with some illustrations
of what goes wrong when parameters are unidentified or only weakly identified.

I’m not quite sure how to address the problem here, though.
Anyone else have any ideas?

- Bob

I am not quite sure i understand the problem. I am well aware that some of the intercepts will have minimal influence on the measurement value, and that is exactly the case. I have included some, plus their interactions, to show these have no effect. E.g. that the measurement value does not vary regardless of age and gender.

If this is not the “correct" way of doing it, then I am open for suggestions. Would it be better to have a group wide prior on each nominal variable?

Cheers,

David

messages.body_plain:
Your model’s OK theoretically, but it presents
computational issues due to weak identifiability.

You can subtract a constant from a0_raw and add it
to any of the other a… vars, such as aS_raw and get exactly
the same likelihood.  Therefore the likelihood’s not identified.

Adding normal(0,1) priors technically gives you identification,
but it’s weak.  What are the scales of the parameters you’re getting?
It may help to standardize them.

There’s an example of just how this works and
how it slows things down versus a properly identified model in
the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual (it also shows
why a truly unidentified model won’t work in Stan even though it
may appear to be working [even though it isn’t] in BUGS/JAGS).

Also, adding means to the coefficients won’t work here as they
will also be unidentified.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Your model isn't well-identified as it's written, but it isn't because of a0_raw, but rather because of your inclusion of distinct means for each of your random effects. You should have one non-zero mean for all of your random effects, and no intercept *or* a global intercept and all zero-mean random effects. My suggestion would be to change the block:

|
 a0 <- a0_raw * a0sigma + a0_raw_mean;
  aS <- aS_raw * aSsigma + aS_raw_mean;
  a1 <- a1_raw * a1sigma + a1_raw_mean;
  a2 <- a2_raw * a2sigma + a2_raw_mean;
  a3 <- a3_raw * a3sigma + a3_raw_mean;
  a4 <- a4_raw * a4sigma + a4_raw_mean;

  a1a2 <- a1a2_raw * a1a2sigma + a1a2_raw_mean;
  a1a4 <- a1a4_raw * a1a4sigma + a1a4_raw_mean;
  a2a4 <- a2a4_raw * a2a4sigma + a1a2_raw_mean;
  a1a2a4 <- a1a2a4_raw * a1a2a4sigma + a1a2a4_raw_mean;
|

to:

|
 a0 <- a0_raw * a0sigma + a0_raw_mean;
  aS <- aS_raw * aSsigma;
  a1 <- a1_raw * a1sigma;
  a2 <- a2_raw * a2sigma;
  a3 <- a3_raw * a3sigma;
  a4 <- a4_raw * a4sigma;

  a1a2 <- a1a2_raw * a1a2sigma;
  a1a4 <- a1a4_raw * a1a4sigma;
  a2a4 <- a2a4_raw * a2a4sigma;
  a1a2a4 <- a1a2a4_raw * a1a2a4sigma;
|

while eliminating lines 127 through 135 and 81 through 89.

Also, for clarity's sake, you should be putting your upper bounds on your sigma parameters in the parameter block, like so:

|
real<lower=0,upper=100> a0sigma;
|

Rob

messages.subject: StanBox by Julia
messages.subject_clean: StanBox by Julia
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  We had a recent discussion on the Stan list about building some sort of wrapper for Juliabox so that it could run Stan.  Rob Goedman responded by showing how it is possible to run Stan on the Juliabox, illustrating with two example notebooks.  This was helpful in that it demonstrated the all-important technical capacity of Juliabox to fit Stan models on the web.  But I realized that I was looking for something more in the user interface, something which would allow the user to interact with Stan more directly without having to worry about notebooks or Julia code.

Attached is a sketch of a possible StanBox interface.  It includes one column of inputs and one column of outputs.

The inputs are dominated by a window that holds a Stan program.  Then another window that allows the user to input, inspect, and alter data objects, a small window with config options, and then buttons to push to compile or run the Stan program.

The outputs include a small window of “console” output, showing warnings, errors, and progress of compilation, adaptation, and simulations.  Then a text output giving summary inference for the parameters.  Ideally this would be clickable so that additional information would be available as needed, and of course it should also be possible to dump all the simulations into a file.  Also a graphical output window with some menu options so the user can make traceplots, 2-d traceplots, scatterplots, etc., as desired.

The idea is that, from the user’s perspective, the user is just running Stan (through Julia).

What do people think?
A

  * editable text box: Stan program

  * config / input checks

  * reading data or program from a file (no graphics on
    Andrew’s mockup)

using Shiny (an R tool) and they already have a working
demo of what the graphical menu and visualizations could be.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

A place with shared code would be great to have. As far as I recall there were plans to extend the testing framework to contributed code? Ideally users would provide fancy Stan functions along with tests (& documentation). Collecting this somewhere would be wonderful for the community.

Thinking out loud - a cran like thing for Stan contributed code would be a dream. This would of course include that the code fragements get tested by the tests they were submitted with. In turn this would provide a reliable Stan users library tested with each released Stan release. If a submitted code fragment would fail the tests, it would of course be the responsibility of the supplier to fix it.

This may sound far fetched, but having this would be outstanding and with Jenkins such things should be manageable(?).

Any plans in this direction?

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] StanBox by Julia
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] StanBox by Julia
messages.body_plain:
Great suggestion, and a very useful email trail (copied below as some might not have reached all lists). And thank you Viral for stepping in!

A couple of important points made in these emails jump out to me:

1. Being able to quickly find, duplicate (to make a small change) and compare previous runs is crucial. Initially dropping “History” for a proof of concept might be ok, but it shouldn’t be an afterthought. Could we leverage the new documentation features in Julia to document ‘cases’ in addition to the already available filing capability on JuliaBox?

2. Seamlessly allowing more complex settings/options, possibly by allowing a user to replace (a part of) the “Inputs” column by an editor. Several of the ’skipped’ features could be addressed that way, e.g. the Stan code and data are already in files (Stan.jl uses make to see if a new compilation is required).

3. Graphics, graphics, graphics… In the current ‘chalkboard’ proposal there is space for maybe a single key graphic to be displayed. Maybe more complete graphical output can be shown in additional browser tabs/windows?

As Viral already mentioned, above items rely on Canvas.jl.

4. Currently Stan.jl works on CmdStan level. With RCall.jl and/or Cxx.jl it might become possible to drill deeper, but those require Julia 0.4.

I need to get some Galerkin stuff to work over the next 3 months, but would be happy to use remaining cycles to further (or open up) Stan.jl as needed for ‘StanBox by Julia’.

And I’ll certainly take a look at Shiny to see what could be mixed into Stan.jl (which uses Mamba.jl’s features for posterior and graphical analysis).

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@mac.com

> On Feb 2, 2015, at 11:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> A minimal proof of concept would be:
>
>  * editable text box: Stan program
>
>  * editable text box: data
>
>  * button: run program on data using default sampling
>
>  * output text box: whatever Stan.jl prints as it goes
>
>  * output text box: whatever Stan.jl provides to print
>      the posterior (print() in RStan; print command in CmdStan)
>
> This skips:
>
>  * graphical output & menus for controlling it
>
>  * user-specified config for Stan
>
>  * history
>
>  * config / input checks
>
>  * reading data or program from a file (no graphics on
>    Andrew’s mockup)
>
> There’s a group here working on Stan posterior visualization
> using Shiny (an R tool) and they already have a working
> demo of what the graphical menu and visualizations could be.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  I have a soft spot in my heart for hand-drawn
> UI mockups.  This one’s especially fun because I
> last saw it in chalk on the board in our office.

Daniel & Sebastian,

In Julia the convention is to name github packages with the extension .jl. I wonder if a similar approach could work for Stan.

If contributed Stan code projects would all be named xxxx.stan they are easy to find on github.

Over time capabilities like Iain’s http://pkg.julialang.org could be added, possibly some of the user code testing could migrate to Travis (e.g https://travis-ci.org/goedman/Stan.jl ) and documentation to ReadTheDocs (e.g.  http://stanjl.readthedocs.org/en/latest/ ).

Just a suggestion. Clearly not free as someone would have to figure out how to install Stan on travis-ci for testing, etc. But having worked with both Cran and the Julia package ecosystem maybe worth to investigate.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@mac.com

messages.body_plain:
The NIMBLE project at Berkeley is working on something
like blocked sampling based on a BUGS-like directed
graphical modeling language:

http://r-nimble.org/

I’m not sure what they’re doing for sampling now, but
we’ve talked to them about including Stan’s HMC/NUTS
as a compilation target.

Within Stan, we don’t have a design for how we’d express
discrete models.  The challenge is to efficiently compute their
conditional distribution based on the continuous parameters.
In a directed graphical model, it’s easy to compute the
Markov blanket.  With Stan’s imperative programming language,
it’s less clear.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

It’s still not a high priority for us because we don’t
work with many discrete models where it’s not possible
to marginalize out the discrete parameters.  When you can
do the marginalization, it’s a huge win over actually
doing the sampling.  (I understand that it’s complicated
compared to writing a BUGS program.)

The one place where we can’t really do the marginalization
explicitly is with counts, but about the only place
we imagine using that is with missing count data.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
What Andrew is suggesting may appear to work in BUGS/JAGS
but it absolutely won't work in Stan.  See the chapter of
the manual on problematic posteriors for an extended discussion
of what's going on with the posterior.

If z is a K-dimensional parameter vector constrained so that

  sum(z) = 0,

then you can code up z as follows:

  parameters {
    simplex[K] z_raw;
    real<lower=0> z_scale;
  ...

  transformed parameters {
    vector[K] z;
    z <- (z_raw - 0.5) * z_scale;
  ...

The parameterization involves K free parameters (K-1 for the
simplex and one for the scale).

There's a discussion in the manual of how to parameterize models
like IRT so that they are identified.

In the simplest case, if you have something like a 1PL IRT
model, with likelihood:

 y[m,n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha[m] - beta[n]))

then alpha and beta aren't identified.  But if you give them
priors such as

  alpha ~ normal(0,1);
  beta ~ normal(0,10);

then you'll find in the posterior, alpha will sum to 0 and
beta will float because it's less constrained.  That's our
recommended strategy for dealing with centering.  It's not
a hard constraint.

An alternative is to pin one of the elements of alpha or
beta, and let everything adjust relative to that.  This is
clunkier to code, but possible.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
[re-inserted OP in BCC]

We have to put this all in context.  Let's assume
we're talking about parameters for an IRT model.

If the goal is to identify the model by using

> alpha_adj <- alpha - mean(alpha)

and then using alpha_adj in the likelihood rather than alpha,
it just won't work in Stan.  Read the problematic posteriors
chapter of the manual for both examples and theory.  The synopsis
is that NUTS will run off forever and never turn around if
the parameter alpha isn't identified in the model.  It's
not enough for the transformed parameter to be identified.

As Andrew says, using a centered prior on alpha with a constrained
scale relative to beta will only roughly center each posterior draw.
But it will identify the model in the sense Andrew describes in
his regression book with Jennifer.

Also, if you do a penalized MLE, you should get the alpha properly
centered if beta gets an uninformative prior.

  alpha ~ normal(0,1)

  beta ~ uniform(-inf,inf)

This lets the alpha identify the scale and location (in the sense
of "identify" Andrew talks about in his regression book with Jennifer),
while letting beta float.  This is the direction Sophia Rabe-Hesketh
recommended because in IRT models the focus is usually on the test
questions (beta), not the students (alpha).  Of course, we'd more usually
put a hierarchical prior on beta in Bayesian models:

  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);

- Bob

On Wednesday, February 4, 2015 at 10:46:46 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The remaining question in my mind is then what we should be
> doing for priors.  Should the prior be on z or z_free?

With that construction, we are basically saying

f(z | theta) = f(z_free | theta) * f(z[K] | z_free)

and the last term is conditionally deterministic given the sum-to-zero constraint.

So, I think specifying f(z_free | theta) as the prior is usually okay, particularly, if you are using multivariate normals. f(z | theta) would have a singular covariance matrix and the easiest way around that is to go to a full-rank subspace.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Degenerate_case

Ben

On Thursday, February 5, 2015 at 1:04:46 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But won't it produce a different prior based on which of
> the z[k] is defined as the negative sum of the others?

If you imagine a KxK covariance matrix that is singular, then yes, depending on which row / column you exclude, the remaining elements of the (K-1)x(K-1) covariance matrix differ but I don't think the distribution of z changes unless you are doing something informative with the priors that go into the linear predictor.

This paper actually argues for using sum-to-zero constraints in discrete choice models

http://www.burgette.org/sMNP-R0-FINAL.pdf

relative to the usual practice of defining utility relative to a baseline category largely because which category you decide to call the baseline affects the predictions. We can do a similar posterior is Stan but without the Gibbs sampling.

> then there's some implication of double-prioring the

> what the implication is marginally if I say z ~ normal(0,1).
> (I could probably figure it out with some effort, and
> it'd be easy to investigate computationally.)

The wikipedia link explains how to do a K-dimensional density with a singular covariance matrix, but Stan does not have an easy way for users to do a generalized inverse or pseudo-determinant.

Ben

messages.subject: Stan and CmdStan v2.6.0 released
messages.subject_clean: Stan and CmdStan v2.6.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Stan and CmdStan v2.6.0 is out now. Download links can be found from the home page:

  http://mc-stan.org

If you have any trouble, please contact us on the stan-users group. The other interfaces will be released soon.

- Stan Dev Team

v2.6.0 (5 February 2015)
======================================================================

New Features
----------------------------------------
* log_mix function for binary mixtures [half of #970]
* neg_binomial_2 CDF function [#1129]

Language Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* allow local-variable integers to be treated as constants,
  allowing, among other things, more general ODE functions [#1131]
* initialize transformed data and generated quantities the
  same way as transformed parameters [#1099]
* libstan.a removed and model compilation is 100% header-only [#1095]
* check for infinite/nan inits from boundary initializations
  with warning [#537]

API/Build/Test Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* removed extra variables being generated by validation [#1248]
* generalize OperandsAndPartials to second order [#676]
* rationalize error handling, using const char* args for efficiency [#1234]
* upgrade to Boost version 1.55 library [#1206]
* generate .hpp instead of .cpp for models [#803]
* value_of_rec recursive metaprogram to pull values out of higher-order
  autodiff structures; removes order dependency on fwd/rev includes
  [#1232]
* tests now run more efficiently with Python script [#1110]
* add performance tests to continuous integration to perform
  end-to-end regression testing on speed [#708, #1245]
* manual index parser for tool automation in interfaces (such as
  auto-complete suggestions) and emacs mode
* refactor log determinant and fix return type cast in vector arena
  alloc  [#1187]
* update makefile dependencies for auto-generated cpp test files [#1108]
* move test models into clearly labeled directories (good/bad) [#1016]
* removing policies from math error checking [#1122]
* remove usage of Boost's formatting (which can cause runtime
  errors like printf) [#1103]
* rearrange directory structure of err_handling [#1102]
* clean up math includes to proper location in source tree [#778]
* remove Windows newline and write script to catch in future [#1233]
* remove extra copy of Eigen (3.2.0), leaving just Eigen 3.2.2 [#1206]
* remove example-models dependency from Git [#1105]

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------------
* allow identifiers with prefixes matching keywords [#1177]
* allow functions to be used in variable declaration constriants [#1151]
* fix segfault resulting from multivariate normal in optimizer (root
  cause wasn't in optimizer, but in autodiff nesting cleanup) [#1200]
* fixed return type in language and C++ for append_row of two
  column vectors and append_col of two row vectors [#1241]
* fixed derivative error for pareto_type_2_log() [#1223]
* remove unused models from stan distribution (they're now in
  the stan-dev/example-models repo on GitHub) [#1249]
* squash compiler warnings and fix windows tests (mostly
  signed vs. unsigned, as usual) [#1257]
* fix memory leak in ODE solver [#1160]
* fix overflow in gamma_p function to throw instead [#674]
* make sure multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose returns a symmetric
  matrix [#1121]
* fix overflow in Poisson RNG to throw instead [#1053]

Documentation
----------------------------------------
* manual updated for 2.6 [#1081]
  - new chapter on software process (thanks to Sebastian Weber
    and Tony Rossini for help)
  - new chapter on sparse and ragged arrays
  - pointers to Julia and MATLAB interfaces (yay!)
  - vectorization of CDFs described
  - fix priors on IRT models
  - added discussion of multiple change points
  - remove range-contstrained scale priors
  - clarified fixed parameter call
  - remove references to "std::vector" in favor of "array"
  - corrected signs for lasso and ridge and discuss truncated gradient
    and absolute zero results
  - extended discussion of Gaussian process priors (thanks
    to Aki Vehtari, Jon Zelner, and Herra Huu)
  - remove bogus paths to models and replace with pointers to
    example-models repo
  - clarified Wishart/inverse Wishart parameterizations w.r.t. BDA3
  - fixed exp_mod_normal definition
  - fix student-t reparameterization
  - fix hurdle distribution definition

Thanks!
----------------------------------------
Thanks to all the users who contributed code and doc corrections
and comments: Alex Zvoleff, Juan Sebastián Casallas, Gökçen
Eraslan, seldomworks [GitHub handle], Avraham Adler, Sebastian
Weber, Amos Waterland, David Hallvig, Howard Zail, Andre Pfeuffer,
Bobby Jacob, Cody Ross, Krzysztof Sakrejda, Andrew Ellis, John Sutton

messages.body_plain:
I missed this in the release notes:

  * fixes memory leak in multivariate normal

It was taken care of as a side-effect of fixing our autodiff
stacks (that is, the bug wasn't in multivariate normal but
lower level).

I'd also like to officially welcome our newest core developer, Rob Trangucci.
He's behind the new log_mix function:

  log_mix(theta, lp1, lp2) =def= log(theta * exp(lp1) + (1-theta) * exp(lp2))

It has the log_sum_exp behavior built in.  There's a vector-based version
in the works, too.

Rob also sped up autodiff (and hence sampling and optimization) by 5--10% by
tightening up the argument validation routines.

- Bob

messages.subject: Potential Collaboration Work: using STAN for Fisheries Stock Assessment - model parsimony vs parameter estimation.
messages.subject_clean: Potential Collaboration Work: using STAN for Fisheries Stock Assessment - model parsimony vs parameter estimation.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan-users.  See below.  If this project interests anybody, feel free to contact Allan Debertin directly.
A

>> On Jan 28, 2015, at 11:11 AM, Allan Debertin <adeb...@uoguelph.ca> wrote:
>>
>> Dear Dr. Andrew Gelman,
>>
>> I am a PhD candidate at the University of Guelph, in Guelph, Canada and my thesis investigates mechanisms that could explain why the Ontario Lake Erie Gillnet Fishery persists to harvest top-trophic level fishes, whereas in other systems top-trophic level fisheries have collapsed. One of my thesis chapters gathers fishery stock assessments for two different species White Perch (non-native to Lake Erie) and White Bass to estimate the total abundance of these species through a time series.
>>
>> The theme of the stock assessment chapter is to examine the trade-offs between model complexity towards parameter estimation and parsimony of model information. Model complexity affects reliability in two important ways. Use of low-parameter models may mask underlying dynamics such that harvest policies deemed to be conservative actually lead to greater risk, or vice versa. However, decision-making based on over-parameterized models may similarly put stocks at risk, leading to pleas for model parsimony.  To evaluate reliability, three stock assessment models will be ranked in retrospective analyses using information theoretic approaches. We expect to see with increasing model complexity we would have have better parameter estimates (e.g. smaller credible intervals), however, we expect an inverse relationship with parsimony (i.e. as models become more complex, we would expect greater Information Criterion scores).
>>
>> I was going to use JAGS to run three state-space stock assessment models, i) surplus production model (least complex), ii) age-structured sequential population model, iii) an integrated, age-structured, length-based model (most complex) to gather parameter estimates and rank these model using Deviance Information Criterion (DIC). However, the DIC scores for the most complex models are negative (suggests a poor model fit), and I've read a few articles that WAIC may be more useful information criterion when comparing non-nested models.
>>
>> I have developed code in STAN to calculate WAIC for the first two models i) surplus-production model and ii) age-structured sequential population models, but I am having difficulty properly coding the third iii) integrated model. I'm not even sure if it can be coded in STAN due to looping structures that require sequential order of command lines in STAN. I have been reading and have posted a few articles on the STAN google forum, and noticed that you are now a proponent of STAN, and in particular the use and development of easier to use WAIC calculations. I'm wondering, if you would be interested in helping me with developing the proper coding in STAN for the last integrated-stock assessment model to determine the WAIC. If so, I would offer co-authorship on any potential peer-reviewed journal articles.
>>
>> Let me know if you are interested in this collaboration and I can send the code I have been working on for all three models. We should also a schedule a online meeting to go through the troubleshooting of the code, since I would like to understand STAN a little better.
>>
>> Best regards,
>>
>> Allan Debertin
>> --
>> Allan Debertin, MSc
>> PhD Candidate
>> Integrative Biology
>> University of Guelph
>

I am a bit unsure if this is the way to go. As I mentioned, what I am really interested in with this model is to estimate the effect from the random effects on the measurement. E.g., is there an negative, zero or non-zero effect from age on the measurement value. If I add a random intercept to the baseline value (a0), I am not really sure if the suggested model is describing what I am actually interested in. On the other hand, the commonly accepted knowledge about these coefficients is actually that they should have close to zero effect on the measurement.

What it make more sense if I split up the model into three, one for each phenotype? Currently, I have combined three (related) phenotypes (type) in the model, which leads to the three way interaction term (age*sex*type).

Would it help to re-evaluate the priors on the standard deviation for each random effect? I can imagine there are more suitable priors for e.g. gender rather than just a uniform one.

On a somewhat unrelated note, is there a smart "trick" in STAN for converting these standardised nominal coefficients back to their original scale?

Cheers,
David

> |

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I suspect I already know the answer to my question, but I wanted to see if users had something to offer that I'm not seeing.

I have latent covariates (with an associated Stan sampling statement, of course) and want a flexible predictive model of these covariates, so I'm considering typical basis expansions of these covariates.  Cubic B-splines seem expedient, but the usual basis expansion has discontinuous (Haar) and other basis functions that have non-smooth kinks.  I'm thinking: no problem IF my covariates are known (no sampling statement), but non-diff basis functions of latent covariates blows me out of the water with regard to the gradient operations for typical Stan algorithms.  Is this correct?  Do I have to seek differentiable basis functions (e.g., Gaussian kernels) of latent quantities, or is there some sort of work-around to use, e.g., B-spline basis functions in this scenario?

Best,

Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
I had been struggling last year using Stan with a particular type of model where firms are organized in a sector and industry hierarchy, but also by countries. So there's two hierarchies in it. At the time, I didn't know what it was called, but I just found out it is called a cross-classified model. I found a reference here:

Rasbash, J. and Goldstein, H. (1994) Efficient analysis of mixed hierarchical and cross classified random structures using a multilevel model. Journal of Educational and Behavioural Statistics, 19: 337-350.

Bristol University seems to have a decent amount of materials on this. The documentation for MLwiN discusses this approach. Their examples correspond well to the school example from Stan, except that it adds in a neighborhood.

I'm curious if anyone has tried anything like this in Stan.

Missing data/ partially complete data points are imputed using a Poisson counting process, leading to a probability mass that doesn't conform to any simple distribution. I can fix the problem in a not-so-hacky way by fitting a scaled beta distribution to the estimates, but since this converts the integral values to continuous ones, I can't use a negative binomial outcome distribution. A gamma outcome distribution won't work because I have some true zeros.

Is there a continuous generalization of the Negative Binomial?

Is there any way to make this work in Stan, or am I going to have to relearn JAGS?

>>>
>>> Dear Dr. Andrew Gelman,
>>>
>>> I am a PhD candidate at the University of Guelph, in Guelph, Canada and my thesis investigates mechanisms that could explain why the Ontario Lake Erie Gillnet Fishery persists to harvest top-trophic level fishes, whereas in other systems top-trophic level fisheries have collapsed. One of my thesis chapters gathers fishery stock assessments for two different species White Perch (non-native to Lake Erie) and White Bass to estimate the total abundance of these species through a time series.
>>>
>>> The theme of the stock assessment chapter is to examine the trade-offs between model complexity towards parameter estimation and parsimony of model information. Model complexity affects reliability in two important ways. Use of low-parameter models may mask underlying dynamics such that harvest policies deemed to be conservative actually lead to greater risk, or vice versa. However, decision-making based on over-parameterized models may similarly put stocks at risk, leading to pleas for model parsimony.  To evaluate reliability, three stock assessment models will be ranked in retrospective analyses using information theoretic approaches. We expect to see with increasing model complexity we would have have better parameter estimates (e.g. smaller credible intervals), however, we expect an inverse relationship with parsimony (i.e. as models become more complex, we would expect greater Information Criterion scores).

>>> Let me know if you are interested in this collaboration and I can send the code I have been working on for all three models. We should also a schedule a online meeting to go through the troubleshooting of the code, since I would like to understand STAN a little better.
>>>
>>> Best regards,

messages.body_plain:
I've read Gelman and Hill, actually a few times at this point. It focuses on the hierarchical case. Cross-classification might be thought of as multilevel, but it is not the same thing as hierarchical.

To flesh out what I was saying above a bit more, consider the basic school example that is used in the RStan Quick Start guide (among other places). Imagine that there is also a neighborhood grouping, such that a student from school A could be a member of neighborhood A, but another student from school A could be a member of neighborhood B. A student from school B similarly could be from neighborhood A or B. So the grouping is not nested/hierarchical. From a social science perspective, this might be relevant in some cases.

The approach corresponds to my firm/sector/country example because you might have firms that have similar characteristics because they are in the same sector or because they are int he same country. My alternative was to just make a hierarchical decision to go country->country_sector->country_industry. However, you're implicitly assuming that sector A in country A is uncorrelated with sector A in country B, which is not the case.

When I was previously trying to estimate the cross-classification structure in Stan (i.e. not the hierarchical one), my problem was that it was overidentified. I had a mean for country and a mean for sector in the mean equation and they would blow up.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Cross-Classified Models in Stan
messages.body_plain:
What Michael said.  You just have to make sure not
to create an identifiability problem.  For instance, if
you have a simple multilevel model with voters grouped by
state of residence and by sex, then you can have a
varying-intercept model for each, but they should both get
0 means because you'll have a general intercept and all you model
by group is difference from the "mean" behavior of the group.

So you'd have alpha1 varying by state, alpha2 varying by sex,
and a single parameter alpha for an intercept:

  y[n] ~ inv_logit(alpha1[state[n]] + alpha2[sex[n]] + alpha);
  alpha1 ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha1);
  alpha2 ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha2);
  sigma_alpha1 ~ ...
  sigma_alpha2 ~ ...
  alpha ~ ...

If you try to assign a hierarchical mean for alpha1 and alpha2, the
model's not identified.  This isn't Stan, it's just a fact about
the likelihood.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan and CmdStan v2.6.0 released
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan and CmdStan v2.6.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Sure, here's simple mixture of normals we used to test the function:

data {
  int<lower = 0> N;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0, upper = 1> theta;
  vector<lower = 0>[2] sigmas;
  vector[2] means;
}
model {
  theta ~ beta(6,4);

  sigmas ~ normal(1,2);

  means[1] ~ normal(10,1);
  means[2] ~ normal(-1,1);

  for(i in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(log_mix(theta,normal_log(y[i],means[1],sigmas[1]),
                              normal_log(y[i],means[2],sigmas[2])));
}

Rob

Hi Bob,

Thanks for the note.  I’m semi-encouraged to code my own basis functions in the function block and see what happens.  OK may be OK.  But, I’ll let the list speak first, and may contact Aki, too.

Perhaps there is no problem.  Suppose I consider y ~ N(f(x), sigma), where f(x) = h1(x)b1 + … + hp(x)bp, and x is latent (has its own sampling statement), and h1…hp are the B-spline basis function representation for piecewise cubic polynomial splines (for some specified number of knots or df) evaluated at x.  The confusing thing to me is that, in this case, some of the basis functions are discontinuous (piecewise constant, e.g., Haar functions or top hat functions, whatever), with others being triangle functions and others smoother.  But, f(x) is differentiable!  After all, f(x) consists of piecewise cubic polynomials that are made to match in their first few derivatives at knot points.  So, from this perspective, someone might say there is no problem. But, if you think about distributing the differential operator across the (relatively conceptually unattractive but computationally (in some contexts) attractive) B-spline basis functions, hj, then some of these hj are not differentiable (granted only at few points).  I’m not sure which is the correct Stan perspective.

Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hi—somebody, Bob I think it was, told me it’s a bad idea to put blocks of code within if-statements, this sort of thing:

if (flag){
 . . .
 . . .
}

where “flag” is then passed in as data, and ypu pass in a 1 if you want that section of code to be run.  Bob was saying this is a bad idea, it’s better just to have new Stan programs.

I just want to say that, from the user’s perspective, this can be tricky.  In a lot of my work now I’ll have 5, say, very slightly different Stan programs—the basic model is the same but there are some differences for example with error distributions or priors or auxiliary data.  It’s not so horrible to have 5 different programs.  But then if I need to make a change, I have to go thru and edit all 5.  This is a recipe for error and it violates the “never duplicate your code” principle.  It’s possible that some of this could be ameliorated using functions.  But for now, I have to say that if-blocks are a convenient way for me to keep some control over my sprawling workspace.

A

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that was me.  I agree that cut-and-paste is really bad
news.  It's nearly impossible to maintain.  And also hard to
understand.  Making code readable is very important.

What I was objecting to in particular about Andrew's use of
conditional model blocks was that in one of the branches, there was a
parameter that wasn't used.  Andrew's Stan program was something like

|
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
...
model {
  if (cond) {
    theta ~ ...;
  }
...
|

where the only use of the parameter theta in the model was inside
the conditional.  Andrew could get away with this trick because theta
is constrained and thus has a proper posterior even with no sampling
statement in the model.  But this trick won't work if theta is
unconstrained, because the posterior will be improper.

What we really need is a way to encapsulate the use and the declaration
together.  Then we could have something like a grouped predictor,
associated parameter vector, and linear predictor term modularly
declared as data, parameter, and term in the model.  But I have no idea
how to modularize that way.

- Bob

see if you can see anything wrong --- it looks properly
coded and the data generation looks OK to me, so I don't see why it's
not working.  Thanks.

(If I get some time, I'll try to write one of my own from
scratch and see if I can get it working.)

Stan should certainly be able to fit such a model.  Lots
of people have implemented mixtures of varying components.

If you don't plan to generalize beyond two components, I'd
recommend simplifying to a beta prior, using log(theta) and
log1m(theta) and the two-argument log_sum_exp, or even better,
the new log_mix() function.   But that shouldn't be the problem.

You also want to change this:

>  transformed parameters{
>    matrix[D,D] var_cov[K];
>    for (m in 1:K){
>      var_cov[m] <- diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m]) * diag_pre_multiply(tau[m],L_Omega[m])';
>    }
>  }

There is a multiply_self_transpose() function that's much more
efficient than using diag_pre_mulitply twice.  But
if you're going to use a Cholesky parameterization, you can
just go all the way and use multi_normal_cholesky.  But again, this
is just an efficiency issue.

If you have a dirichlet(1) prior, you can just drop it.  The
default is a uniform prior over the parameters as declared (here
that'd be uniform over simplexes).  Again, just an efficiency issue.

- Bob

I don't know if there was anything new on the R side per se,
but here's release notes for Stan itself.  It was mostly a bug
fix release for memory leaks and cleaning up the code under the hood.

- Bob

v2.6.0 (5 February 2015)
======================================================================

New Features
----------------------------------------
* log_mix function for binary mixtures [half of #970]
* neg_binomial_2 CDF function [#1129]

Language Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* allow local-variable integers to be treated as constants,
  allowing, among other things, more general ODE functions [#1131]
* initialize transformed data and generated quantities the
  same way as transformed parameters [#1099]
* libstan.a removed and model compilation is 100% header-only [#1095]
* check for infinite/nan inits from boundary initializations
  with warning [#537]

API/Build/Test Enhancements
----------------------------------------
* removed extra variables being generated by validation [#1248]
* generalize OperandsAndPartials to second order [#676]
* rationalize error handling, using const char* args for efficiency [#1234]
* upgrade to Boost version 1.55 library [#1206]
* generate .hpp instead of .cpp for models [#803]
* value_of_rec recursive metaprogram to pull values out of higher-order
  autodiff structures; removes order dependency on fwd/rev includes
  [#1232]
* tests now run more efficiently with Python script [#1110]
* add performance tests to continuous integration to perform
  end-to-end regression testing on speed [#708, #1245]
* manual index parser for tool automation in interfaces (such as
  auto-complete suggestions) and emacs mode
* refactor log determinant and fix return type cast in vector arena
  alloc  [#1187]
* update makefile dependencies for auto-generated cpp test files [#1108]
* move test models into clearly labeled directories (good/bad) [#1016]
* removing policies from math error checking [#1122]
* remove usage of Boost's formatting (which can cause runtime
  errors like printf) [#1103]
* rearrange directory structure of err_handling [#1102]
* clean up math includes to proper location in source tree [#778]
* remove Windows newline and write script to catch in future [#1233]
* remove extra copy of Eigen (3.2.0), leaving just Eigen 3.2.2 [#1206]
* remove example-models dependency from Git [#1105]

Bug Fixes
----------------------------------------
* allow identifiers with prefixes matching keywords [#1177]
* allow functions to be used in variable declaration constriants [#1151]
* fix segfault resulting from multivariate normal in optimizer (root
  cause wasn't in optimizer, but in autodiff nesting cleanup) [#1200]
* fixed return type in language and C++ for append_row of two
  column vectors and append_col of two row vectors [#1241]
* fixed derivative error for pareto_type_2_log() [#1223]
* remove unused models from stan distribution (they're now in
  the stan-dev/example-models repo on GitHub) [#1249]
* squash compiler warnings and fix windows tests (mostly
  signed vs. unsigned, as usual) [#1257]
* fix memory leak in ODE solver [#1160]
* fix overflow in gamma_p function to throw instead [#674]
* make sure multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose returns a symmetric
  matrix [#1121]
* fix overflow in Poisson RNG to throw instead [#1053]

Documentation
----------------------------------------
* manual updated for 2.6 [#1081]
  - new chapter on software process (thanks to Sebastian Weber
    and Tony Rossini for help)
  - new chapter on sparse and ragged arrays
  - pointers to Julia and MATLAB interfaces (yay!)
  - vectorization of CDFs described
  - fix priors on IRT models
  - added discussion of multiple change points
  - remove range-contstrained scale priors
  - clarified fixed parameter call
  - remove references to "std::vector" in favor of "array"
  - corrected signs for lasso and ridge and discuss truncated gradient
    and absolute zero results
  - extended discussion of Gaussian process priors (thanks
    to Aki Vehtari, Jon Zelner, and Herra Huu)
  - remove bogus paths to models and replace with pointers to
    example-models repo
  - clarified Wishart/inverse Wishart parameterizations w.r.t. BDA3
  - fixed exp_mod_normal definition
  - fix student-t reparameterization
  - fix hurdle distribution definition

Thanks!
----------------------------------------
Thanks to all the users who contributed code and doc corrections
and comments: Alex Zvoleff, Juan Sebastián Casallas, Gökçen
Eraslan, seldomworks [GitHub handle], Avraham Adler, Sebastian
Weber, Amos Waterland, David Hallvig, Howard Zail, Andre Pfeuffer,
Bobby Jacob, Cody Ross, Krzysztof Sakrejda, Andrew Ellis, John Sutton

- Bob

messages.subject: things I learned from doing a Stan demo in an intro class
messages.subject_clean: things I learned from doing a Stan demo in an intro class
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I did an unrehearsed live demo of Stan in my survey sampling class and I learned some interesting things.

I started with linear regression.  I had code that I’d copied from an earlier Stan manual in which the model was not vectorized.  With 1000 data points it ran really slow.  So I think it’s a really good thing that in the current Stan manual, we start with the vectorized version and then only give the non-vectorized later.  Otherwise people will use the slow code and think that Stan is slow.

Then I explained the output.  I have mixed feelings about showing the Monte Carlo standard error.  At one level, it’s a good thing to know.  But for a practitioner it’s a bit of a distraction.  In practice, all the user really needs to know is that this MCSE is less than 1/10 (say) of the posterior se.  So I’m wondering if we actually need a new summary, not quite R.hat but this other thing. Or maybe it’s fine to just use R.hat because, in practice, if R.hat is less than 1.1, the MCSE is probably so low that we don’t need to worry about it.  Then a similar issue with all the quantiles and effective sample size:  it’s more trouble to explain that it’s worth.  I think the basic output should be estimate, sd, and some summary of OK-ness (R.hat or something else).  And for this I’m not just thinking of basic users.  Even advanced users such as myself, when we’re doing applied statistics, we usually just want an estimate, and uncertainty, and an indication that we can trust the computation.  The only thing I’m still undecided on is whether to use mean & sd, or median & quantiles.  Right now I’m leaning toward reporting the median as the estimate, and reporting the half-width of the central 68% interval as the standard error.  But I’m open to persuasion on this.

Next I decided, just for fun, to fit a nonlinear model:  y = a*exp(-b*x) + c + error, with N(0,sigma) errors.  I simulated some data (x taking on the values between 0 and 23, setting a=.5, b=1/10, c=1, sigma=.2, and I fit it constraining all the parameters to be positive. (In retrospect I’m thinking I should’ve just constrained b and sigma to be positive; constraining a and c made sense in the context of my hypothetical example, but in general it’s poor practice to put in hard constraints unless absolutely necessary.)

I simulated data and fit the model and all was fine.  But then I repeated and the fit blew up, I was getting some estimates of b that were either really close to 0 (1e-10, etc) or really high (1e10, etc), I can’t remember which.  The point is that there can be instability at the extremes, and I realized the model need a bit of hand-holding.  As a kluge I constrained b to be between 1/50 and 1 (which made sense in the context of the example).  A hard constraint was ugly but was easy enough to understand.  I didn’t want to confuse the class by introducing a normal prior here.

So this second example was a bit of a mess.  Which suggests to me that in the manual/book we need to throw in an example to explicitly address instability and constraints.  Since, ultimately, this is an inherent difficulty with modeling, it’s not anything to do with Stan in particular.

A

I'm afraid I don't really speak Python, but I could understand
what you're doing and recreate it in R.  I didn't try to debug
what you did, but I'm attaching our recommended approach to
dealing with multivariate normals along with some simulation
code in R that successfully fits the mixture.

Here's the Stan program, which I just hardcoded to two
mixture components.

mix.stan
-----------------------------------------------
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=1> D;
  vector[D] y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
  vector[D] mu[2];
  cholesky_factor_corr[D] L_Omega[2];
  vector<lower=0>[D] sigma[2];
}
transformed parameters {
  cholesky_factor_cov[D] L_Sigma[2];
  for (k in 1:2)
    L_Sigma[k] <- diag_pre_multiply(sigma[k], L_Omega[k]);
}
model {
  theta ~ beta(1,1);
  for (k in 1:2) {
    sigma[k] ~ cauchy(0,2);
    L_Omega[k] ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
    mu[k] ~ normal(0,5);
  }
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real lp1;
    real lp2;
    lp1 <- multi_normal_cholesky_log(y[n], mu[1], L_Sigma[1]);
    lp2 <- multi_normal_cholesky_log(y[n], mu[2], L_Sigma[2]);
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp1,
                                   log1m(theta) + lp2));
  }
}
generated quantities {
  cov_matrix[D] Sigma[2];
  for (k in 1:2)
    Sigma[k] <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Sigma[k]);
}
-----------------------------------------

This works out to uniform priors on the mixture ratio theta and
also on the correlation matrices.

Here's the simulator, using same parameters as Vasileios, but more
data:

sim.R
-----------------------------------
library(MASS);

mu1 <- c(7,9);
Sigma1 <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 2), 2, 2);

mu2 <- c(15,17);
Sigma2 <- matrix(c(2, 0.1, 0.1, 2), 2, 2);

y <- rbind(mvrnorm(200,mu1,Sigma1), mvrnorm(600,mu2,Sigma2));
N <- dim(y)[1]
D <- 2;
-------------------------------

Note that it's four times as many samples.  Covariance
matrices are notoriously difficult to estimate.  If you
use the data sizes you started with, the covariances won't
even be as well estimated as they are with 200 and 600 data
points.

Here's the code to run it in R:

fit.R
-----------------------------------------
library(rstan);

fit <- stan("mix.stan", data=c("N","D","y"),
            control=list(stepsize=0.001),
            chains=1, iter=1000,
            seed = 7654321);
------------------------------------------

Note that I set the initial stepsize to 0.001.  This is often a good
idea in complex models to cut down on Hamiltonian simulation errors early
in warmup.

That's not bad, but you can see that the posterior on the covariance terms
is still fairly wide.

What I would suggest you do going forward is modify this code to use
the Dirichlet and make sure you get the same answer with two components.
Then generalize to more components.

Then you could enrich other parts of it.  But it's best to leave everything
parameterized as is using the Cholesky factors.

In Stan 2.6, if you only need two components, you should replace

    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp1,
                                   log1m(theta) + lp2));

with

    increment_log_prob(log_mix(theta, lp1, lp2));

> On Feb 9, 2015, at 7:43 PM, Vasileios Stampoulis <vasileios....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>
> I cannot thank you enough for your help!
>
> Your R-script runs like a charm and apparently using more data in my python code seems to work as well. I 'll check whether something funny goes on with the numerical precisions in python.

It's not Python --- all the sampling happens on the C++
side.

It may have something to do with initialization.  And
also initial step size.

> My final model will be a mixture of 4 distributions and the dataset is large (300,000 datapoints and it's 4-dimensional). I 'll be more than happy to post it assuming that it works fine and of course cite Stan.

That'd be great.  It should work in 4D with 300K data points, but
it'll be around 600 times slower, so rather than a minute, it might
take 10 hours to fit an n_eff of 500 --- it'll probably converge faster
with that much data.

Multiple chains are a problem with these mixtures because of
identifiability of indexes --- there's a discussion in the problematic
posteriors chapter of the manual, but no good solution.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
If you can build a model of the overdispersion, you can
use that directly.  But I'd be nervous about a linear
variance formula with a negation --- you might want to
use the log link function in a GLM to characterize it.

The negative binomial is a compound Poisson-gamma :-)
The best way to implement a compound distribution like
the negative binomial (or student-T) is to integrate out
the latent parameter.  If you can't do that, then you
can just code everything up explicitly using the latent
parameters, but it can be much slower sampling.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] goodness of fit/full predictive posterior/mixed predictive posterior
messages.body_plain:
I would suggest option A, cross-validation, which gets straight
to predictive power and is easily interpretable across frameworks.
You'd want to use full Bayesian inference for the predictions,
of course.

Between options B and C, usually the likelihood is defined by
marginalizing out the hierarchical parameters for the prediction,
so C seems more reasonable.  And it's necessary to make predictions
for new groups not part of the original fit.  This is tricky in more
highly structured multilevel models.

We need to add more discussion of posterior predictive checks
and cross-validation to the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Compound Poisson in stan
messages.body_plain:
I'm not exactly sure what you're looking for, but
you can [Poisson regression overdispersion] on the web.

I have an econometrics book that covers count data in detail:

http://www.amazon.com/Regression-Analysis-Econometric-Society-Monographs/dp/1107667275/

I've only got the first edition, but it has a lot of info
on regression for overdispersion.

The basic idea is that you can model the overdispersion just
like you model the mean.

- Bob

> On Feb 11, 2015, at 8:30 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob
>
> Is it possible to provide some reference how to use the model for overdispersion directly in stan?  I would like to explore this idea first.  By the way, glm(y~x+x^2-1,family=gaussian(link="log")) gave me 1e-5 as a coefficient for x and -1e-12 for x^2.
>
> Thank you,
> Linas
>
>
> On 2/10/2015 11:55 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> If you can build a model of the overdispersion, you can
>> use that directly.  But I'd be nervous about a linear
>> variance formula with a negation --- you might want to
>> use the log link function in a GLM to characterize it.
>>
>> The negative binomial is a compound Poisson-gamma :-)
>> The best way to implement a compound distribution like
>> the negative binomial (or student-T) is to integrate out
>> the latent parameter.  If you can't do that, then you
>> can just code everything up explicitly using the latent
>> parameters, but it can be much slower sampling.
>>
>>
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>

On Wed, Feb 11, 2015 at 11:39:07AM -0800, Steve wrote:
> Bob:
>
> I'm not sure the best way to address this, but here is a copy of the
> statements and output that produced these summaries. I'm not sure that the
> "monitor" code does exactly what a print(stan.fit) does, but it did seem to
> extract and summarize (half of) the right chains. But I don't know why only
> half.

as.array extracts the chain after warmup, that is, the second half by default.
monitor has an argument warmup that is set to half length of the chain.
If you apply monitor to what is extract samples from stanfit, warmup should be
set to zero. These are all documented.

Jiqiang

I was looking at the ?as.array help file - the right help file is ?as.array.stanfit which specifies the non-warmup samples are coerced to an array.

To get closer to my original request of an equivalent to "print(stanfit.object, chains=c(1,2))", by borrowing from Ben one can use "monitor(extract(fit.log.mix,permuted=F,inc_warmup=T)[,c(1,2),,drop=F],digits=2)"

As Bob pointed out, the lp__ means are very different. This maybe due to the first two chains converging to a minor mode of the posterior instead of the major(?) mode to which the last two chains converged. There were two means and two SDs giving four possible label switches, and (I believe) four posterior modes. The similarity of the se's might indicate that the inference is valid even when the chains converge to the minor mode. Does anyone have further insight into these issues (lp__ mean v. different, se's same after label switch - validity of inferences at minor modes)?

logit(Mu[y,a,i]) <-alphav[i]+beta[i]*L[y,a];

be translated to STAN as:

> On Feb 13, 2015, at 1:53 AM, Allan Debertin <alland...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> My Apologies for not being clear. The local variable assignments aren't an issue. And don't worry about L, it's part of the more complex model above and that part is working fine.
>
> I'm more interested in the functions I changed. STAN only works if you assign functions to right-hand side, not the left.

Right --- it's like a programming language that way.

> So in the example above would the JAGS function:
>

> logit(Mu[y,a,i] <-alphav[i]+beta[i]*L[y,a];

>
> be translated to STAN as:
>

> Mu[y,a,i]<-inv_logit(alphav[i]+beta[i]*L[y,a];

Correct.  But if you're going to use Mu as a parameter
for a Bernoulli or binomial, then we have ones that
are parameterized on the logit scale.  So rather than:

  y ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha));

you can write:

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha);

The suffixes indicate the parameter scale.

> Two other JAGS to STAN function conversion questions:
>
> 1) inprod() function in JAGS, is the inner product of a matrix. It seems that in STAN, this function is not necessary.
>
> So, does this in JAGS:
> s[y,a] <-inprod(ge[j], sg[y,a,j]);
>
> Translate to STAN as:

> s[y,a] <-ge[j]*sg[y,a,j];

I always get confused with this inner and outer notation.

What are the types of ge[j] and sg[y,a,j] and how do you
define the result?

> 2. Finally, I have a question about matrix division, particularly a matrix divided by a vector.
> So in JAGS this statement works and produces numbers:
> pc[y,a] <-g[y,a] /delta[y] //delta[y] is sum(g[y,a]
>
> Whereas in STAN does not... what function do I need to use in STAN to have a matrix divided by a vector.
>
> would it be the "./" command?
> pc[y,a] <-g[y,a] ./ delta[y] //delta[y] is sum(g[y,a]

Our matrix division is the usual one:

  A/B  = A * inverse(B)

  B\A  = inverse(B) * A

JAGS followed R in straying from usual notation and I
have no idea what "/" does in JAGS, but if it's like R,
they're using the usual operators for the pointwise ones.

We don't allow matrix ./ vector, only matrix ./ matrix.

The allowable function signatures are all laid out explicitly
in the manual.

- Bob

Dear Bob et al.,

I am reopening this thread from about 8 months ago. Back then I received a “vanishing density” error message during initialization that I wasn’t ab to resolve. In the meantime I continued working with JAGS, where my model compiles and samples without a problem.

Now with Stan 2.6 released I thought I’d give this a try again. The model still won’t initialize, but now I get a new error message (full log is attached):

Error :

Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.

 Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.

error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

(see attached error_stan26.log)

Afaik, I did the first two recommendations: I initialized all variables in the parameters block (see run_model.r, attached) and I also constrained the underlying values. I also changed the parameterization of variance of the group distribution to a half-cauchy (rpdf_cauchy.stan). All of this had no effect. I still get the above mentioned error message.

I have two questions:
1. Do you or anyone else have another idea that I can try to get Stan to estimate this model.

2. Following, Ahn et al., J Neurosci, Psycho Econ, 2011, I parameterized the group distribution with a beta distribution that was restricted to a uni-modal distribution by limiting the variance parameter. The reason for this choice was that two parameters have natural boundaries between 0 and 1. The two parameters (a,b) of this beta were itself parameterized in terms of mean and variance, which were also drawn from a beta. (see attached code rpdf.stan for the exact implementation).

Do you think that this is a good way to parameterize the model or should I use a different group distribution? Is is possible that the choice of distributions is causing this initialization failure in Stan?

Thanks a lot,
Jan

n_divergent is the number of divergent iterations during a
Hamiltonian trajectory.  When NUTS is implemented corrected
it rejects dynamically at the first divergent iteration so when
using NUTS (the Stan default) n_divergent should be 0 or 1.
But that is not guaranteed (we may not be using NUTS and
NUTS may not be implemented correctly).

You'll have to write that code by hand.  Stan doesn't
automatically broadcast like R does.  The reason is that
it's a very dangerous coding practice because of the way it
hides potential errors.

Here's a function that should work (I haven't tried to
compile or test it):

matrix row_div(matrix a, vector b) {
  matrix[rows(a), cols(a)] result;
  for (m in 1:rows(a))
    result[m] <- a[m] / b[m];
  return result;
}

Or you could just write the same thing inline in the code
where you need it.

Of course, requiring users to write loop-based code is also
error prone, but we decided that was the better course than
potentially hiding errors.  What we really need is a unit-testing
framework for Stan functions so that users could debug them before
dropping them into models.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Stan can definitely get stuck around a mode.

Diagnosing multiple modes is one of the motivations for using
multiple chains with diffuse starting points and using R-hat;
if they don't all converge to the same point, sampling around
multiple modes is one possible culprit.

For full Bayesian inference, you need to integrate over
the entire posterior.  So if there are a few modes, you need
to visit each in proportion to its posterior mass.  If there
are a combinatorially daunting number of posterior modes,
full Bayesian inference just isn't possible.

It's not enough to just do inference around one, though it's common
to do that in machine learning circles (e.g., with Gibbs
samplers for LDA, which are combinatorially multimodal).

This is a very very tricky business to get
right from a Bayesian perspective.  Michael Betancourt's working
on some sampling techniques that'll work for a few modes.

There aren't even algorithms for finding the best modes in
general, because it's an NP-hard problem (i.e., no known
sub-exponential algorithm and every reason to believe there
will never be sub-exponential algorithms).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yes, in general, sampling from multiple modes in posteriors (I could imagine) is NP-hard. What I wondered was whether for finite mixtures, the minor modes were "reflections" of the major mode due to symmetry between label switches, and if that's the case, then sampling from a minor mode will give the same SEs (and full posterior inference) that either sampling from the major mode would, or even sampling in proportion to their weight from all modes. This thought arose from the observation that in this case (mixture of two normals - two means, two SDs - with four modes), sampling from one of the minor modes gave exactly the same SEs as sampling from the major mode. In the two sub-groups of chains c(1, 2) and c(3, 4), Rhat was uniformly 1, indicating convergence within the sub-group, while Rhat when evaluated over all four chains ranged from 8 to 71 over the parameters.

Thanks to Rob for the log_mix function, to Ben for the inference method for a sub-group of chains, and to Bob for pointing out the lp__ mean difference and the discussion. Looking forward to the full implementation of #970.

On Saturday, February 14, 2015 at 4:44:53 PM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Stan can definitely get stuck around a mode.
>
> Diagnosing multiple modes is one of the motivations for using
> multiple chains with diffuse starting points and using R-hat;
> if they don't all converge to the same point, sampling around
> multiple modes is one possible culprit.
>
> For full Bayesian inference, you need to integrate over
> the entire posterior.  So if there are a few modes, you need
> to visit each in proportion to its posterior mass.  If there
> are a combinatorially daunting number of posterior modes,
> full Bayesian inference just isn't possible.
>
> It's not enough to just do inference around one, though it's common
> to do that in machine learning circles (e.g., with Gibbs
> samplers for LDA, which are combinatorially multimodal).
>
> This is a very very tricky business to get
> right from a Bayesian perspective.  Michael Betancourt's working
> on some sampling techniques that'll work for a few modes.
>
> There aren't even algorithms for finding the best modes in
> general, because it's an NP-hard problem (i.e., no known
> sub-exponential algorithm and every reason to believe there
> will never be sub-exponential algorithms).
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
The point is that full Bayesian inference marginalizes over the modes, so you have
to sample _all_ of them, not just one.  What people often really want is to sample
conditioned on a label assignment, which is a fundamentally different problem
with no immediate answer.

A second complication is that in mixture models there tend to be a bunch of
side modes in addition to the combinatorial label-reswitching modes, and these
are _not_ invariant to permutations.

On Feb 14, 2015, at 9:19 AM, Steve <ssk...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Yes, in general, sampling from multiple modes in posteriors (I could imagine) is NP-hard. What I wondered was whether for finite mixtures, the minor modes were "reflections" of the major mode due to symmetry between label switches, and if that's the case, then sampling from a minor mode will give the same SEs (and full posterior inference) that either sampling from the major mode would, or even sampling in proportion to their weight from all modes. This thought arose from the observation that in this case (mixture of two normals - two means, two SDs - with four modes), sampling from one of the minor modes gave exactly the same SEs as sampling from the major mode. In the two sub-groups of chains c(1, 2) and c(3, 4), Rhat was uniformly 1, indicating convergence within the sub-group, while Rhat when evaluated over all four chains ranged from 8 to 71 over the parameters.
>
> Thanks to Rob for the log_mix function, to Ben for the inference method for a sub-group of chains, and to Bob for pointing out the lp__ mean difference and the discussion. Looking forward to the full implementation of #970.
>
> On Saturday, February 14, 2015 at 4:44:53 PM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Stan can definitely get stuck around a mode.
> >
> > Diagnosing multiple modes is one of the motivations for using
> > multiple chains with diffuse starting points and using R-hat;
> > if they don't all converge to the same point, sampling around
> > multiple modes is one possible culprit.
> >
> > For full Bayesian inference, you need to integrate over
> > the entire posterior.  So if there are a few modes, you need
> > to visit each in proportion to its posterior mass.  If there
> > are a combinatorially daunting number of posterior modes,
> > full Bayesian inference just isn't possible.
> >
> > It's not enough to just do inference around one, though it's common
> > to do that in machine learning circles (e.g., with Gibbs
> > samplers for LDA, which are combinatorially multimodal).
> >
> > This is a very very tricky business to get
> > right from a Bayesian perspective.  Michael Betancourt's working
> > on some sampling techniques that'll work for a few modes.
> >
> > There aren't even algorithms for finding the best modes in
> > general, because it's an NP-hard problem (i.e., no known
> > sub-exponential algorithm and every reason to believe there
> > will never be sub-exponential algorithms).
> >
> > - Bob

messages.body_plain:
>>
>> The point is that full Bayesian inference marginalizes over the modes, so you have
>> to sample _all_ of them, not just one.  What people often really want is to sample
>> conditioned on a label assignment, which is a fundamentally different problem
>> with no immediate answer.
>>
>
> Is the problem with what happens between the modes?  I'd
> assume if the troughs between the modes were deep enough,
> and they were all just label switching symmetries, then
> sampling one would be good enough.

The problem is that full Bayes says to integrate, which means average over
all of the modes.  Means will typically put you in the middle of all those modes
in one of those troughs you mention, with the variance spanning the set of
all modes.  Mathematically this is correct, it’s just not what people typically
implicitly want.

What people really want in practice is to do model comparison (averaging
over a bunch of unimodal models can give multimodal marginal posteriors)
which they hack by saying things like “pick a mode”.  But that’s not really
all that well-posed outside of the model comparison perspective.

In what sense?  It's a different model for reasons outlined in my last mail
(no intercept, K coefficient vectors instead of (K-1)).

It's just the Bayesian posterior for the model you defined.

The main issue is identifiability because with K coefficient vectors, if you
add a constant to each one, you get the same answer.  Of course, without an
intercept, you don't have a plain old additive term.

We were wrestling about which formulation to use, K versus (K-1), but
they both have their strengths and weaknesses.  The nice part about (K-1)
is that it's identified even if there's an intercept.  The nice part about
K is that it's symmetric in the categories, so the prior applies to all of them.

- Bob

Dear Andrew and Bob,

thanks for taking up this issue again. I really appreciate the prompt and immediate support thatt you provide on this list.

@Andrew
Yes, this is a left-over from running the model in JAGS. I also wanted to be really sure that I don’t run into extreme values in the beta, when trying to figure our this problem. But I will certainly use natural bounds and vague, but not flat priors when I really get this model to run in Stan.

@Bob
Thanks a lot for getting the devs involved. I am also gone until the middle of next week, so no need to hurry this. In the mean time, I’ll will make the model simpler by eliminating some  parameters and possibly also the choice function in the model, which now selected similarly to a softmax.

Are there any other internal variable (besides lp__) that you need for debugging?

Btw, the model is the one from Bishara et al., J Math Psychol, 2010 for the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test. The description of the model is terrible though (within the text), but it works.
doi:  10.1016/j.jmp.2008.10.002
free @ http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2872109/

Thanks a lot,
Jan
