messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] computing pi (and volume of a hypersphere) with Stan using Monte Carlo integration
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] computing pi (and volume of a hypersphere) with Stan using Monte Carlo integration
messages.body_plain:
Hi, maybe a good comparison would be to then do the very same model but with x and y as parameters, so that Stan does HMC on this (simple) space.  Then the answers can be compared.

> On Feb 14, 2015, at 10:15 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Here's a Stan program I wrote for the Machine Learning
> Summer School in Sydney next week to illustrate how
> Monte Carlo integration can be used to compute the
> mathematical constant pi.  This is THE textbook example
> of Monte Carlo.
>
> /**
> * Compute the mathematical constant pi by Monte Carlo integration.
> *
> * First, sample (x,y) uniformly from a square with vertices (-1,1),
> * (-1,1), (1,-1), (1,1) by sampling x and y independently from the
> * interval (-1,1).
> *
> * Second, determine if (x,y) lies within the circle circumscribed in
> * the square, by testing if (x^2 + y^2 < 1). Then multiply the
> * proportion of points inside the circle by the area of the square (4 here)
> * to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of the area of the circle.
> *
> * A circle with radius r has area pi * r^2, so setting r=1, yields
> * an area of pi.
> *
> * NOTE: Run with fixed parameter algorithm and zero warmup iterations.
> */
> model {
> }
> generated quantities {
>  real<lower=-1,upper=1> x;
>  real<lower=-1,upper=1> y;
>  real<lower=0,upper=4> pi;
>  x <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>  y <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>  pi <- 4 * (x^2 + y^2 < 1);
> }
>
> You could actually eliminate x and y by defining
>
>  pi <- 4 * (uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 + uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 < 1);
>
> but I left them in because I thought it'd be useful to be able
> to plot the draws (for instance, with one color inside the circle
> and another outside).
>
>
> Here's how I called it in RStan:
>
>> fit <- stan("pi.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param",iter=1e4,warmup=0)
>
> and here's the fit:
>
>> print(fit)
> Inference for Stan model: pi.
> 4 chains, each with iter=10000; warmup=0; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=40000.
>
>     mean se_mean   sd  2.5%  25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
> x    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 40000    1
> y    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 39364    1
> pi   3.14    0.01 1.64  0.00  4.0   4 4.0  4.00 40000    1
>
>
> I wouldn't enter any digit competitions for pi with MC integration,
> because the error only goes down at a rate of O(1/sqrt(M)) where M is the
> number of MC draws, so each decimal place requires on the order of
> 100 times more samples.  The nice thing about pure Monte Carlo (as
> opposed to Markov chain Monte Carlo) is that each draw is independent,
> so n_eff should be equal to the sample size (it won't be exactly that
> because of the approximate nature of the n_eff calc, which doesn't
> know MC was in play).
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Here's a more general program to compute the volume of
> a hypersphere:
>
> /**
> * Compute the volume of a hypersphere of a given radius in a
> * given number of dimensions by Monte Carlo integration.
> *
> * The volume will be the mean of the sampled sphere_volume values.
> */
> data {
>  int<lower=1> N;
>  real<lower=0> radius;
> }
> transformed data {
>  real cube_volume;
>  cube_volume <- (2 * radius)^N;
> }
> model {
> }
> generated quantities {
>  vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[N] x;
>  real<lower=0,upper=cube_volume> sphere_volume;
>
>  for (n in 1:N)
>    x[n] <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>
>  sphere_volume <- cube_volume * (dot_self(x) < radius);
> }
>
> If you feed it data (N=2, radius=1), you get the same result as
> the simpler program in the main body of this e-mail.
>
> I probably won't have time to do the more general case in class.
>
> P.P.S.  This is totally going in the manual :-)
>

> --

is a terrible summary, because all the draws of pi are
either 0 or 4.  So medians aren't going to work well for
any discrete distribution, like a Bernoulli, because you'll
get 0 or 1 (or maybe 1/2 if you have the same number of
0s and 1s and you interpolate).

>>> * Second, determine if (x,y) lies within the circle circumscribed in
>>> * the square, by testing if (x^2 + y^2 < 1). Then multiply the
>>> * proportion of points inside the circle by the area of the square (4 here)
>>> * to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of the area of the circle.
>>> *
>>> * A circle with radius r has area pi * r^2, so setting r=1, yields
>>> * an area of pi.
>>> *
>>> * NOTE: Run with fixed parameter algorithm and zero warmup iterations.
>>> */
>>> model {
>>> }
>>> generated quantities {
>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> x;
>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> y;
>>> real<lower=0,upper=4> pi;

>>> }

>>> pi <- 4 * (uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 + uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 < 1);

>>> but I left them in because I thought it'd be useful to be able
>>> to plot the draws (for instance, with one color inside the circle
>>> and another outside).
>>>
>>>

>>>> fit <- stan("pi.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param",iter=1e4,warmup=0)
>>>
>>> and here's the fit:
>>>
>>>> print(fit)

>>> post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=40000.
>>>

>>> x    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 40000    1
>>> y    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 39364    1
>>> pi   3.14    0.01 1.64  0.00  4.0   4 4.0  4.00 40000    1

>>>
>>> I wouldn't enter any digit competitions for pi with MC integration,
>>> because the error only goes down at a rate of O(1/sqrt(M)) where M is the
>>> number of MC draws, so each decimal place requires on the order of
>>> 100 times more samples.  The nice thing about pure Monte Carlo (as
>>> opposed to Markov chain Monte Carlo) is that each draw is independent,

When explaining this one, it perhaps would be helpful to emphasize that this is a somewhat atypical example in that the inference of interest is for the expectation of a binary predictive quantity, rather than a parameter or function of parameters.

>>>> * to produce a Monte Carlo estimate of the area of the circle.
>>>> *
>>>> * A circle with radius r has area pi * r^2, so setting r=1, yields
>>>> * an area of pi.
>>>> *
>>>> * NOTE: Run with fixed parameter algorithm and zero warmup iterations.
>>>> */
>>>> model {
>>>> }
>>>> generated quantities {
>>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> x;
>>>> real<lower=-1,upper=1> y;
>>>> real<lower=0,upper=4> pi;
>>>> x <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>>>> y <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>>>> pi <- 4 * (x^2 + y^2 < 1);
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> You could actually eliminate x and y by defining
>>>>
>>>> pi <- 4 * (uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 + uniform_rng(-1,1)^2 < 1);
>>>>
>>>> but I left them in because I thought it'd be useful to be able
>>>> to plot the draws (for instance, with one color inside the circle
>>>> and another outside).
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Here's how I called it in RStan:
>>>>
>>>>> fit <- stan("pi.stan", algorithm="Fixed_param",iter=1e4,warmup=0)
>>>>
>>>> and here's the fit:
>>>>
>>>>> print(fit)
>>>> Inference for Stan model: pi.
>>>> 4 chains, each with iter=10000; warmup=0; thin=1;
>>>> post-warmup draws per chain=10000, total post-warmup draws=40000.
>>>>
>>>>  mean se_mean   sd  2.5%  25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
>>>> x    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 40000    1
>>>> y    0.00    0.00 0.58 -0.95 -0.5   0 0.5  0.95 39364    1
>>>> pi   3.14    0.01 1.64  0.00  4.0   4 4.0  4.00 40000    1
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> I wouldn't enter any digit competitions for pi with MC integration,
>>>> because the error only goes down at a rate of O(1/sqrt(M)) where M is the
>>>> number of MC draws, so each decimal place requires on the order of
>>>> 100 times more samples.  The nice thing about pure Monte Carlo (as
>>>> opposed to Markov chain Monte Carlo) is that each draw is independent,
>>>> so n_eff should be equal to the sample size (it won't be exactly that
>>>> because of the approximate nature of the n_eff calc, which doesn't
>>>> know MC was in play).
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>> P.S.  Here's a more general program to compute the volume of
>>>> a hypersphere:
>>>>
>>>> /**
>>>> * Compute the volume of a hypersphere of a given radius in a
>>>> * given number of dimensions by Monte Carlo integration.
>>>> *
>>>> * The volume will be the mean of the sampled sphere_volume values.
>>>> */
>>>> data {
>>>> int<lower=1> N;
>>>> real<lower=0> radius;
>>>> }
>>>> transformed data {
>>>> real cube_volume;
>>>> cube_volume <- (2 * radius)^N;
>>>> }
>>>> model {
>>>> }
>>>> generated quantities {
>>>> vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[N] x;
>>>> real<lower=0,upper=cube_volume> sphere_volume;
>>>>
>>>> for (n in 1:N)
>>>> x[n] <- uniform_rng(-1,1);
>>>>
>>>> sphere_volume <- cube_volume * (dot_self(x) < radius);
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> If you feed it data (N=2, radius=1), you get the same result as
>>>> the simpler program in the main body of this e-mail.
>>>>
>>>> I probably won't have time to do the more general case in class.
>>>>
>>>> P.P.S.  This is totally going in the manual :-)
>>>>

You beat me to it on the pstream being Stan-generated.  The processing we're doing is a little weird here: stan code -> stan compiler -> .cpp -> RcppAttributes -> different .cpp -> compiler

The way the 'as' template specialization is written now, it the second argument to 'normalize' would have to be a pointer to the correct stream generated on the C++ side, passed to R as an XPtr (this ends up being the 'externalptr' class.  I ran the function by saying I had one and then passing a null pointer

I have no idea how the plumbing of streams works on the rstan side...

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a better way to code this zero-inflated model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a better way to code this zero-inflated model?
messages.body_plain:
The coding will affect efficiency, but not the posterior.

Why is it surprising the random effects are skewed (I don't have
much experience here).

For coding tips, the biggest one is to follow the multivariate
normal example for random effects in the regression chapter of the manual.
We finally wrote up our recommended practices for efficiency and priors.
Inverse Wishart isn't your friend --- it's only standard practice in
BUGS/JAGs because they can only handle conjugate multivariate distributions.

You also want to vectorize wherever possible.  So

  for (m in 1:M)
    vu[m] ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);

should be:

  v ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);

I'd also stay away from beta(0.01,0.01) priors unless you have some
reason for wanting to push the posterior toward the boundaries.

 for (i in 1:P)
    zeros_beta[i] <- 0.0;

can be reduced to

  zeros_beta <- rep_vector(0, P);

I don't have the patience to work it out, but if you could replace

  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (m in 1:M)
      for (b in 1:B)
        u[(m-1)*B+b] <- vu[m][b];

with matrix operations, it'd most likely be faster.

Replace

poisson_log(y[n], exp(eta))

with poisson_log_log(y[n], eta);

poisson_log() takes its parameter on the log scale, and poisson_log_log is
the function.

- Bob

Skewness in parameters with normal priors can arise when there is uncertainty in the group-level variance.  The 8-schools example illustrates.

> On Feb 15, 2015, at 8:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> The coding will affect efficiency, but not the posterior.
>
> Why is it surprising the random effects are skewed (I don't have
> much experience here).
>
> For coding tips, the biggest one is to follow the multivariate
> normal example for random effects in the regression chapter of the manual.
> We finally wrote up our recommended practices for efficiency and priors.
> Inverse Wishart isn't your friend --- it's only standard practice in
> BUGS/JAGs because they can only handle conjugate multivariate distributions.
>
> You also want to vectorize wherever possible.  So
>
>  for (m in 1:M)
>    vu[m] ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);
>
> should be:
>
>  v ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);
>
> I'd also stay away from beta(0.01,0.01) priors unless you have some
> reason for wanting to push the posterior toward the boundaries.
>
> for (i in 1:P)
>    zeros_beta[i] <- 0.0;
>
> can be reduced to
>
>  zeros_beta <- rep_vector(0, P);
>
> I don't have the patience to work it out, but if you could replace
>
>  for (n in 1:N) {
>    for (m in 1:M)
>      for (b in 1:B)
>        u[(m-1)*B+b] <- vu[m][b];
>
>
> with matrix operations, it'd most likely be faster.
>
> Replace
>
> poisson_log(y[n], exp(eta))
>
> with poisson_log_log(y[n], eta);
>
> poisson_log() takes its parameter on the log scale, and poisson_log_log is
> the function.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
There are different arguments threaded through different
types of functions.  See the chapter on user-defined functions
in the manual.

The output stream is where any print() statement will be
rendered.

Any function ending in _rng gets a random-number generator
and is only usable in the generated quantities block.

And any function ending in _log can be used as a log
density using the sampling statement (~) notation with the
first argument on the left.

Any function ending in lp__ has access to the log probability
accumulator and may only be used in the model block.

There's still the issue of whether we want to relax this last
restriction to allow use in the transformed parameters block,
where we (still) allow lp__ --- it was just an oversight on my
part when implementing increment_log_prob() not to include
transformed parameters.

To see better what's going on, look at how the functions
in the following program get compiled:

functions {
  real foo_lp(real x) {
    return x;
  }

  real foo_log(real x) {
    return x;
  }

  real foo_rng(real x) {
    return x;
  }
}
model {
}

In particular, note that foo_log also gets an extra template
parameter for propto.  This just made me realize that although
the propto template parameter is there, there's no way to access
it within the program.  I'll open an issue to make it available
for definining conditionals.

template <typename T0__, typename T_lp__, typename T_lp_accum__>
inline
typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T0__, T_lp__>::type
foo_lp(const T0__& x, T_lp__& lp__, T_lp_accum__& lp_accum__, std::ostream* pstream__);

template <bool propto, typename T0__>
inline
typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T0__>::type
foo_log(const T0__& x, std::ostream* pstream__);

template <typename T0__>
inline
typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T0__>::type
foo_log(const T0__& x, std::ostream* pstream__);

template <typename T0__>
inline
typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T0__>::type
foo(const T0__& x, std::ostream* pstream__);

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.subject_clean: Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.body_plain:
I've been trying to figure out the best way to run Stan in a parallel environment, and I would be very curious to hear people's thoughts on the best ways to choose number of chains and number of iterations. After some experiments, I've come to the conclusion that, if one has access to multiple cores, then it makes sense to set iterations to a value just above the number necessary for convergence, and then run as many chains as are needed for the desired sample size. So for instance, if my model seems to be converging after 500 iterations, I could run 10 chains (each on its own core) with 600 iterations each, set the warmup to 500, and end up with a total sample size of 1000 after combining the chains.

Does this make sense? Are there better ways to approach this? My goal is to parallelize as much as possible in order to optimize speed (and I am dealing with models that otherwise take a long time because of the size of the datasets).

Thanks,
John

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.body_plain:
I am curious how you can determine the number of iterations "just above
the number necessary for convergence". In my experience, diagnosing
(non)convergence is tricky.

My approach is somewhat unscientific, but this is what I do:

1. Build up models gradually, making sure that the results make sense
with the addition of each new component. If something causes a drastic
change, it is suspect.

2. Try to get effective samples, using transformations, the "Matt
trick", etc. Also I try to optimize the Stan program for speed
(vectorization, etc) whenever possible. For the latter, I do test runs
on a single chain, for about 100 iterations, and time them. I have found
profiling with operf & co cumbersome and not really informative, maybe I
am not doing it right, but for my purposes simply benchmarking and
tweaking works fine.

3. If I have achieved reasonably effective sampling, 1000 samples per
chain are often enough for my purposes.

4. Then I run 3 to 7 chains (depending on whether I use my 4-core laptop
or a more powerful multicore server), with overdispersed starting
points, and check convergence diagnostics.

IMO step 3 above is the most work but also provides the largest
benefit. YMMV.

HTH,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
The main problem is that the number of iterations required
for convergence is a function of initialization, and pretty
much impossible to diagnose until you've gone way past what
you need.  Unitl you've made 50 or so draws *after warmup*, it's hard
to diagnose non-convergence.

This is why we haven't automated any of this or
worried too much about restarting.

There's some interesting open research questions around all of
this, such as sharing adapation across chains and minimizing number
of post-warmup chains required to diagnose convergence.  The whole
convergence thing is a can of worms, as you may have gathered if
you're following Ben's and Andrew's and Michael's discussion on
the stan-dev mailing list.

To address Tamas's specific procedure:

(1) by all means, this is the way to go.

(2) ditto.

(4) ditto.

(3) usually, we run until the MCMC std error is an
order of magnitude or so below the posterior std deviation.
And that's usually well below 1000 iterations total unless
we need very precise answers or have a model with difficult geometry
where the effective sample size rate per iteration is low.

We usually get there by doubling.  Start with 100 iterations
total, half warmup, half sampling, and if that's not enough,
start again and double it.  At most you waste about 50% of
your time compared to the absolute ideal (which as Tamas points
out is very hard to diagnose).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Regarding 4: is there a way to make it easier (semi-automated) to run
chains with overdispersed starting points?

I was thinking of something like this: given a posterior distribution of
parameters in the R^n space that Stan uses internally, estimate a
multivariate normal or T, scale up the variance, and draw some initial
values from that.

This would be obvious to implement if it wasn't for the transformation
between R^n and the constrained parameter space: given the posterior I
would need to undo this, and then in rstan I could not find a way to
init with internal R^n values. So mostly now my overdispersed points are
ad hoc.

The recent discussion about convergence was interesting, but at some
point started going over my head. Having a nice canned convergence
metric would be useful I guess, but for me the most reliable indicator
of convergence is stability of results when building up the model
gradually. Writing multiple models used to be very costly for me, Stan
helped a lot here so it is not a big deal any more (surprisingly, now
analysing the results takes more time than programming/running the
model).

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much to both of you - this is all very helpful.

I realize convergence is a big can of worms and I'm probably overly confident when I look at traceplots and rhat values and tell myself that my models have converged. (And I know I can only tell myself that there is no evidence that they have not converged, not that there is evidence they have converged.) I hadn't been following the stan-dev discussion but I will do so now.

I also agree with Tamas about how nice it is to work with Stan in terms of building up models. I had been using BUGS and writing different BUGS code for each model. The key for me has been seeing Germán Rodríguez's suggestion of using a row vector for predictors in Stan and thus making the Stan code much more generalizable: http://data.princeton.edu/pop510/hospStan.html. Perhaps this is also possible with BUGS, and I just hadn't realized it. My approach now is to write one or two different skeletons in Stan code (e.g. a one-level version and a two-level version), and then write a function in R that lets me fit each of these skeletons with different sets of variables. Building up the models then becomes I lot like the way one would approach it with a set of single-level GLMs (apart from the fact that fitting time is usually longer.)

I'm still left with a question about how best to make use of available cores. Say I take all of Tamas's suggestions for optimization, I use Bob's doubling approach to come up with some target number of iterations, I have reason to think that this number will hold for a set of similar models that I am fitting, and someone now gives me access to lots of cores -- like 16 or even 40. How can I take most advantage of those cores? Since increasing the number of chains will speed things up only if I also cut down on iterations, the question is really how to shift work from iterations to chains. From Bob's post, I take it that I should make sure to have at least 50 iterations beyond warmup, otherwise diagnosing non-convergence will be harder. But within that constraint, is it reasonable to shift post-warmup iterations onto extra chains in order to take advantage of the cores?

Thanks again,
John

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Compound Poisson in stan
messages.body_plain:
You need to set the parameters so that you get the desired
mean and variance.

The expectations and variances of both of our negative binomials
are given in the manual.  For example,

  y ~ neg_binomial2(mu,phi)
  E[y] = mu
  var[y] = mu + mu^2 / phi

So if you want

  var[y] = alpha

just set

   alpha = mu + mu^2 / phi

and solve,

   phi = mu^2 / (alpha - mu)

Because phi > 0, this only works for *over*dispersion,
requiring alpha > mu.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.body_plain:
A few comments:

Assuming well-behaved chains (geometric ergodicity and the like)
then running chains in parallel should yield the same inference as
running a full chain, so running in parallel would give you a pretty
solid 1 / cores speed up.

In practice parallel chains are most useful for identifying when
the chains can’t converge or mix efficiently.  I think we’ve focused
(and rightly so) more on robustness than raw performance when
thinking about parallelization.

Most of the time we spend in warmup for Stan is actually focused
on learning the mass matrix and step size — convergence for most
models is _really_ fast.  Eventually we’ll admit user-defiend mass
matrices where you can set a good estimate of the mass matrix
and over all of this tuning overhead when running in parallel.

As Bob notes, the really scalable speedups will come from
internal parallelization of matrix calcs and probability distributions calcs.
But this is going to be haaaaaaard.

On Feb 16, 2015, at 10:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I'm afraid we don't yet have any way to take advantage of multiple
> cores beyond one per chain.  That's going to be on us to
> replace things like matrix operations with parallelized
> version.  Or more ambitiously, to figure out how to
> mulithread the gradient calculations.
>
> Given that warmup takes longer than sampling in most cases,
> it's hard to get much speedup that way --- the upper bound is
> a factor of a bit less than 2.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Feb 16, 2015, at 11:49 PM, John Palmer <johnrb...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Thanks very much to both of you - this is all very helpful.
>>
>> I realize convergence is a big can of worms and I'm probably overly confident when I look at traceplots and rhat values and tell myself that my models have converged. (And I know I can only tell myself that there is no evidence that they have not converged, not that there is evidence they have converged.) I hadn't been following the stan-dev discussion but I will do so now.
>>
>> I also agree with Tamas about how nice it is to work with Stan in terms of building up models. I had been using BUGS and writing different BUGS code for each model. The key for me has been seeing Germán Rodríguez's suggestion of using a row vector for predictors in Stan and thus making the Stan code much more generalizable: http://data.princeton.edu/pop510/hospStan.html. Perhaps this is also possible with BUGS, and I just hadn't realized it. My approach now is to write one or two different skeletons in Stan code (e.g. a one-level version and a two-level version), and then write a function in R that lets me fit each of these skeletons with different sets of variables. Building up the models then becomes I lot like the way one would approach it with a set of single-level GLMs (apart from the fact that fitting time is usually longer.)
>>
>> I'm still left with a question about how best to make use of available cores. Say I take all of Tamas's suggestions for optimization, I use Bob's doubling approach to come up with some target number of iterations, I have reason to think that this number will hold for a set of similar models that I am fitting, and someone now gives me access to lots of cores -- like 16 or even 40. How can I take most advantage of those cores? Since increasing the number of chains will speed things up only if I also cut down on iterations, the question is really how to shift work from iterations to chains. From Bob's post, I take it that I should make sure to have at least 50 iterations beyond warmup, otherwise diagnosing non-convergence will be harder. But within that constraint, is it reasonable to shift post-warmup iterations onto extra chains in order to take advantage of the cores?
>>
>> Thanks again,
>> John
>>
>> On Mon, Feb 16, 2015 at 1:44 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> On Mon, Feb 16 2015, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>>> On Feb 16, 2015, at 11:23 PM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> I was thinking of something like this: given a posterior distribution of
>>>> parameters in the R^n space that Stan uses internally, estimate a
>>>> multivariate normal or T, scale up the variance, and draw some initial
>>>> values from that.
>>>
>>> Isn't that circular?  How do you know what the posterior is?
>>
>> Sorry, I did not mention that I would estimate from a previous run. So I
>> would run the chain twice, once with the default inits, then, based on
>> the results, with the overdispersed inits.
>>
>> This is probably horribly unscientific though and may be a habit that is
>> now not necessary.
>>
>>> Would you mind sharing what were you using before Stan and what the
>>> difficulty was?  I used the same strategy with BUGS/JAGS and the
>>> main problem I had was chains getting stuck without reasonable inits.
>>
>> Custom code with a mix of Gibbs and Metropolis jumps, which was a
>> debugging nightmare but I could make it fast. Now completely superseded
>> by Stan for my purposes.
>>
>> Best,
>>
>> Tmas

On Mon, Feb 16, 2015 at 2:25 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Skewness in parameters with normal priors can arise when there is uncertainty in the group-level variance.  The 8-schools example illustrates.

>
> > On Feb 15, 2015, at 8:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > The coding will affect efficiency, but not the posterior.

> > Why is it surprising the random effects are skewed (I don't have
> > much experience here).
> >
> > For coding tips, the biggest one is to follow the multivariate
> > normal example for random effects in the regression chapter of the manual.
> > We finally wrote up our recommended practices for efficiency and priors.
> > Inverse Wishart isn't your friend --- it's only standard practice in
> > BUGS/JAGs because they can only handle conjugate multivariate distributions.
> >
> > You also want to vectorize wherever possible.  So
> >
> >  for (m in 1:M)
> >    vu[m] ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);
> >
> > should be:
> >
> >  v ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);
> >
> > I'd also stay away from beta(0.01,0.01) priors unless you have some
> > reason for wanting to push the posterior toward the boundaries.
> >
> > for (i in 1:P)
> >    zeros_beta[i] <- 0.0;
> >
> > can be reduced to
> >
> >  zeros_beta <- rep_vector(0, P);
> >
> > I don't have the patience to work it out, but if you could replace
> >
> >  for (n in 1:N) {
> >    for (m in 1:M)
> >      for (b in 1:B)
> >        u[(m-1)*B+b] <- vu[m][b];
> >
> >
> > with matrix operations, it'd most likely be faster.
> >
> > Replace
> >
> > poisson_log(y[n], exp(eta))
> >
> > with poisson_log_log(y[n], eta);
> >
> > poisson_log() takes its parameter on the log scale, and poisson_log_log is

Unless you allocate with new, there's nothing to clean
up.  It'll live on the stack until it goes out of scope,
at which point its destructor will clean it up.

It's another instance of RAII (resource allocation is
initialization --- these C++ folks are very fond of
acronyms).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan in parallel: chains versus iterations
messages.body_plain:
The only way you can guarantee correct sampling is when a single
chain visits every state of high probability — in a multimodal posterior
this means visiting each mode.  Running multiple chains that each
fall into different modes is not helpful as there’s no information on
how to weight the modes relative to each other.

Consequently, _if we assume that our sampler can explore the
entire state space efficiently__ then running multiple chains should
just give a linear speed up.  If we do not have the efficient exploration
then running multiple chains doesn’t offer much help because naively
concatenating their samples does not yield correct inferences.

In practice we get sublinear speed up because of the adaptation
during warmup.  Improving adapting by starting with good initial
values or sharing information between chains should reduce this
overhead and bring you closer to the ideal linear speed up.

But this all assumes that your sampler is ideal.  The most powerful
use of multiple chains is to check for poor convergence or mixing,
and so it’s more about adding robustness than improving speed.

messages.body_plain:
This gives no way to get repeat draws starting from the same seed.  For these extra argument it would be better to make a small C++ function, compiled through sourceCpp, that generates the RNG, wraps it in a Rcpp::XPtr, and passes it to R.  Then on the R side you can pass the same RNG to each of the functions.  I gave the equivalent example for pstream above, but the helper function for this should simply be:

#include <Rcpp.h>

// [[Rcpp::export]]

Rcpp::XPtr<boost::ecuyer1988> get_stream(const int& seed=0) {
  boost::ecuyer1988 base_rng__(seed);
  Rcpp::XPtr<boost::ecuyer1988> ptr(base_rng__);
  return ptr;
}

You can call this in R to get a pointer to the RNG and pass it to any Stan functions that need it.  That way you re-use the same RNG as intended.

Krzysztof

Wasn't sure if you had bigger reasons for going your way so I didn't test the example---sorry.  Here's the right version (also attached in case I mangled the cut-and-paste).

// [[Rcpp::depends(StanHeaders)]]
// [[Rcpp::depends(BH)]]
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEigen)]]
#include <stan/common/command.hpp>

#include <Rcpp.h>

// [[Rcpp::export]]

Rcpp::XPtr<boost::ecuyer1988> get_rng(const int& seed=0) {
  boost::ecuyer1988* base_rng__= new boost::ecuyer1988(seed);
  Rcpp::XPtr<boost::ecuyer1988> ptr(base_rng__,true);
  return ptr;
}

That function (also attached in case I mangled the paste) on the R side will return an 'externalptr' that the _rng functions should be able to share:

> library(Rcpp)
> sourceCpp('get_rng.cpp')
> rng_ptr <- get_rng(0)
> rng_ptr
<pointer: 0x7fff52175860>
> class(rng_ptr)
[1] "externalptr"
> o <- list(); for ( i in 1:1000) {
  o[[i]] <- get_rng(sample.int(n=100, size=1))
}
> str(o)

Does this one work for you? As long as the rng_ptr is not deleted on the R side, it should protect the base_rng__ from getting deleted by the garbage collection.  When the rng_ptr on the R side is deleted, the XPtr takes care of deleting the base_rng__  Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm trying to fit a model given by J groups of observations, and the data within each group is generated according to a normal distribution with an unknown mean and  standard deviation is a linear function of the mean, with unknown slope and intercept.
I want to use "non-informative" priors for all parameters (below I use normal priors with large variance) and I get some problems.
The group means are positive and far from 0 (say >100), and the slope and intercept of the linear relation are constrained to be positive, therefore this guarantees a positive standard deviation.
Below is an example with simulated data. I observe the following issues:

- The Heidelberger-Welch convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter
- The Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter (upper bound of shriink factor > 1.05)
- The 95%-credibilty interval often fail to contain the true value for slope and intercept
- I'm under the impression that convergence does not occur for slope and intercept when looking at the running means (ggs_running(ggsamples, "slope"))

I'd like to have any advice about what I do. Does the model seems sensible to you ? Is there something to do for imrpoving the convergence ?

> library(coda)
> library(rstan)
> library(plyr)
> library(ggmcmc)
>
> # stan model --------------------------------------------------------------
> set_cppo("fast")
mode fast without NDEBUG for compiling C++ code has been set already
> model_code <- "
+ data {
+   int<lower=0> n; // number of observations
+   int<lower=0> J; // number of groups
+   real y[n];
+   int<lower=0> group[n];
+ }
+ parameters {
+   real<lower=0> mu[J];
+   real logintercept;
+   real logslope;
+ }
+ transformed parameters {
+   real intercept;
+   real slope;
+   real<lower=0> sigma[J];
+   intercept <- exp(logintercept);
+   slope <- exp(logslope);

+   }
+ }

+   }
+   for(j in 1:J){

+   }
+   logintercept ~ normal(0,10);
+   logslope ~ normal(0,10);

messages.body_plain:
Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
so far away from standardized.

I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
than hardcoding the priors.

  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.

Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:

> mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)

and then the prior is:

> mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);

This requires the data to pull the posterior
3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
more informative priors, not less informative ones.

As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
a pull to 200.

I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
looks fishy:

> for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> + }

because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
a negative binomial?

This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:

>    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
>    slope <- exp(logslope);
>    for(j in 1:J) {

>      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
>    }

You're better off replacing the last line with:

  sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;

and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:

  vector<lower=0>[J] mu;

Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.

  real<lower=0> slope;
  real<lower=0> intercept;

This would require reformulating the priors.

You can also replace this:

> for(j in 1:J){
> +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> +   }

with the much more efficient

  mu ~ normal(200,30);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Bob, I will try your suggestions.
About the rounding, this is because data are rounded in my real dataset.

Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
> so far away from standardized.
>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.
>
> Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:
>
> > mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)
>
> and then the prior is:
>
> > mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
>
> This requires the data to pull the posterior
> 3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
> are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
> unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
> more informative priors, not less informative ones.
>
> As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
> a pull to 200.
>
> I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
> simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
> R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
> looks fishy:
>
> > for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> > +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> > + }
>
> because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
> are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
> fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
> a negative binomial?
>
> This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:
>
> >    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> >    slope <- exp(logslope);
> >    for(j in 1:J) {
> >      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> >    }
>
>
> You're better off replacing the last line with:
>
>   sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;
>
> and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:
>
>   vector<lower=0>[J] mu;
>
> Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
> you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.
>
>   real<lower=0> slope;
>   real<lower=0> intercept;
>
> This would require reformulating the priors.
>
> You can also replace this:
>
> > for(j in 1:J){
> > +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> > +   }
>
>
> with the much more efficient
>
>   mu ~ normal(200,30);
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Feb 18, 2015, at 10:24 PM, 'Stéphane Laurent' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> > I'm trying to fit a model given by J groups of observations, and the data within each group is generated according to a normal distribution with an unknown mean and  standard deviation is a linear function of the mean, with unknown slope and intercept.
> > I want to use "non-informative" priors for all parameters (below I use normal priors with large variance) and I get some problems.
> > The group means are positive and far from 0 (say >100), and the slope and intercept of the linear relation are constrained to be positive, therefore this guarantees a positive standard deviation.
> > Below is an example with simulated data. I observe the following issues:
> >
> > - The Heidelberger-Welch convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter
> > - The Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter (upper bound of shriink factor > 1.05)
> > - The 95%-credibilty interval often fail to contain the true value for slope and intercept
> > - I'm under the impression that convergence does not occur for slope and intercept when looking at the running means (ggs_running(ggsamples, "slope"))
> >
> > I'd like to have any advice about what I do. Does the model seems sensible to you ? Is there something to do for imrpoving the convergence ?
> >
> > > library(coda)
> > > library(rstan)
> > > library(plyr)
> > > library(ggmcmc)
> > >
> > > # stan model --------------------------------------------------------------
> > > set_cppo("fast")
> > mode fast without NDEBUG for compiling C++ code has been set already
> > > model_code <- "
> > + data {
> > +   int<lower=0> n; // number of observations
> > +   int<lower=0> J; // number of groups
> > +   real y[n];
> > +   int<lower=0> group[n];
> > + }
> > + parameters {
> > +   real<lower=0> mu[J];
> > +   real logintercept;
> > +   real logslope;
> > + }
> > + transformed parameters {
> > +   real intercept;
> > +   real slope;
> > +   real<lower=0> sigma[J];
> > +   intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> > +   slope <- exp(logslope);
> > +   for(j in 1:J){
> > +     sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> > +   }
> > + }
> > + model {
> > +   for(i in 1:n){
> > +     y[i] ~ normal(mu[group[i]], sigma[group[i]]);
> > +   }
> > +   for(j in 1:J){
> > +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> > +   }
> > +   logintercept ~ normal(0,10);
> > +   logslope ~ normal(0,10);
> > + }
> > + "
> > >
> > > # simulate data -----------------------------------------------------------
> > > I <- 6 # number of observations per group
> > > J <- 16 # number of groups
> > > group <- as.integer(gl(16, 6))
> > > a <- 30
> > > b <- 0.1
> > > mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)

If you do it in transformed parameters they will computed once per leapfrog step, whereas in generated quantities it will be once per sample, so it should be more efficient.

messages.subject: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
messages.subject_clean: sparse data matrix, making X*b go fast
messages.body_plain:
I recently modified a model to pre-compute a model-matrix rather than generate it on the fly and pass the model matrix in as data.  What used to be a mess of Stan
functions turns into X * b and I get a nice speed-up even with X being ~50000x200... I did have some issues getting this running (like stan_rdump choking on the 'gsub'
expression but if you remove the gsub commands it works fine).  The model matrix is pretty sparse (>75% 0's) but I understand at the moment there is no sparse data type
in Stan.  I noticed some pointers under the sparse data section of the manual, but I don't see an obvious way of making them apply to the situation where your ultimate
goal is making X * b go fast.

One way of solving it would be to keep the non-zero entries of each row of X, a vector of which entries are non-zero, and code the sparse multiplication by hand.  Are
there any efficiency reasons to make this a function defined in Stan's function block versus coding it in C++ and adding it to Stan's functions?

My question is if I'm missing something here---is there a better way of achieving this?  I'm running a lot of these models and when they were each taking under a day
each it was fine but it seems worth it to do some more optimization now.  I know that X * b could be recoded to do more indexing via functions in the Stan model but
coding new indexing methods all the time in Stan is more error-prone than coding/testing them in R.

Thanks for any suggestions.

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
It is probably hard to get much more speed with just Stan code. If your observations are exchangeable, then maybe it is possible to reorder the observations into groups that each have a common sparseness pattern. If you only pass in the dense columns for each group, you could subset the coefficient vector accordingly so that it is conformable for multiplication with that group's design matrix. Then you are just doing a few matrix-vector multiplications.

Better would be to contribute something in C++. We don't have many sparse matrix operations internally, but we have talked about it. You would probably gain more from utilizing the fact that the Jacobian matrix of eta = X * beta is X than you would from the sparseness.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

If you're using R, you can accomplish that using the "pars" argument in plot, print, and other methods.

e.g.

print(mdl, pars = c("a", "b")) # This only prints the summary of "a" and "b"

or

# This prints the summary of all parameters except "a" and "b"
print(mdl, pars = m@sim$pars_oi[!m@sim$pars_oi %in% c("y_rep")])

You can also specify the parameters you want using pars in the sampling and stan functions, which can be useful when you are generating lots of quantities that may take up too much memory like saving the log_lik, or replications per iteration

Hope that helps,
Juan Sebastian

On Wed, Feb 18, 2015 at 2:07 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I often find that when I am using transformed parameters that are very large, I do not always wish to see them in the plot or print calls in rstan. Plot will usually truncate to only show the first few variables, but if you print a fit that includes a vector transformed parameter with 1000+ entries, you may not even be able to scroll back up to the original parameters. Given the various ways of using Stan, I think a keyword allowing the user to specify the parameters (or transformed parameters or generated quantities) to hide when using plot or print would give the most flexibility. The use of it would be something like
>
>      hide vector[N] Y;
>
> or
>
>      nodisplay vector[N] Y;
>
> or
>
>      someotherkeyword vector[N] Y;
>
> It might also be helpful if there is an ability to toggle this on and off, like with the verbose option when calling the stan function.

messages.body_plain:
I believe the term of art is "nuisance".

Here are three ways to get rid of them.

Let's suppose you have transformed parameter alpha to
save and beta not to save.

transformed parameters {
  real alpha;
  real beta;
  ... define alpha and beta ...
  ...
}

0.  As Juan Sebastián Casallas pointed out, you can
suppress the output from R.

1.  If you don't need beta to compute alpha, it makes
most sense to make it a local variable in the model.

transformed parameters {
  real alpha;
  ... define alpha ...
  ...
model {
  real beta;
  ... define beta ...
  ...
}

The local variables in a model (including everything declared
at the top, are not printed.

2.  The more general approach is to define beta as a local
within the transformed parameters block.

transformed parameters {
  real alpha;
  {
    real beta;  // local variable, won't be printed
    ... define alpha and beta
  }
  ...
}

But that won't work if you actually need beta in the model
block.  You need 1 for that.  But 1 won't always work,
because sometimes you need beta to define alpha efficiently.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
That is a feature, not a bug!

Did you mean to have

  N <- 1

?  I don't see how it'd work with N <- 2, because
Y is only size 1 array/vector.

Unlike R, Stan distinguishes between arrays and
scalars.  One of the reasons R is so inefficient is
that it just converts them freely back and forth.  It's
also a potential source of bugs, because not checking
types can mask programming errors.

I strongly prefer types to be explicit, which is why
Stan's designed how it is.  I expected WAY more pushback
on this from the statisticians than we've gotten, which
makes me very happy.

- Bob

The terminology is confusing.

lognormal is the lognormal distribution.  It has positive
support.  The function is called lognormal_log, because
it evaluates the lognormal density on the log scale.

normal_log is just the standard normal density evaluated
on the log scale.

the program into the error messages.  We have a way forward,
but it's going to take a bit of coding on our part to do
it efficiently.

I'm afraid we don't have sparseness yet.  It's been
part of our recent grant proposals, so if we get one
of those, we'll be on the hook to do it over the
next couple of years.  It requires specifying I/O,
plumbing through the language, and plumbing through
all the interfaces.  Then we actually have to provide
some useful sparse matrix functions, which means a whole
lot more integration with the Eigen sparse matrix lib.
Not fundamentally hard, just a long slog.

If you don't provide customized gradients, there should
be no difference between writing a function in C++ and writing
a function in Stan --- they'll get compiled to the same
underlying C++ in the end.

If you do come up with handy Stan functions, I'm sure
others would appreciate seeing what they are so they could
follow (including me for the manual!).

- Bob

> I believe the term of art is "nuisance".

>
> Let's suppose you have transformed parameter alpha to
> save and beta not to save.
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real alpha;
>   real beta;
>   ... define alpha and beta ...
>   ...
> }
>
> 0.  As Juan Sebastián Casallas pointed out, you can
> suppress the output from R.
>
> 1.  If you don't need beta to compute alpha, it makes
> most sense to make it a local variable in the model.
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real alpha;
>   ... define alpha ...
>   ...
> model {
>   real beta;
>   ... define beta ...
>   ...
> }
>
> The local variables in a model (including everything declared
> at the top, are not printed.
>
> 2.  The more general approach is to define beta as a local
> within the transformed parameters block.
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real alpha;
>   {
>     real beta;  // local variable, won't be printed
>     ... define alpha and beta
>   }
>   ...
> }
>
> But that won't work if you actually need beta in the model
> block.  You need 1 for that.  But 1 won't always work,

In the hierarchical regression example in the manual on page 70, is there a way to impose a truncated prior or distribution on a single element in the beta matrix?  For example, say I have an intercept and a single continuous independent variable.  Essentially, the transformed parameters matrix declaration becomes:

matrix[J,2] beta;  -- a 2 column matrix.

What I am wondering if there is a way to keep the 1st column freely estimated, but constrain the 2nd parameter to have a lower value of zero.  I wish to keep the generalarity of the matrix notation but allow element of that matric to be drawn from truncated distributions.  E.g., real <lower=0> beta[J,2]

Is there any trick to doing this or should I simply create two vectors (2 being my example) where they are defined as

vector[J] beta1
vector<lower=0>[J] beta2

... etc if I have more than two variables...

Thanks,

Tom Eagle

> So it seems like there's room for a limited contribution on the C++ side just to get the sparse version of X*b coded, where X must be data and b's are parameters, with the associated gradients.

This would break our general rule of implementing all
of our functions for arbitrary var/double inputs.
(The only violation of which is for the ODE solver, which
isn't a function so much as a special statement with its
own grammar and error handling/messages.)
If it's implemented, it should allow X to be double
or agrad::var, and b should be able to be double
or agrad::var.

> I can see including sparse operations everywhere is going to be a long slong.  Is there room here for me to do something very limited

Absolutely.  But it needs to be a step toward where we
want to go in the long run.  We want to be able to maintain
backward compatibility as we go.

> --I'm thinking:
>
> a) Stan function to turn a matrix X into a sparse representation

Why would you start with a dense matrix and turn it

problematic here).

you reuse.

messages.body_plain:
There's no way to constrain only part of a
variable.  So you need to define the two vectors
separately (as you show how to do).  The best
way to put them together is then:

  matrix[J,2] beta;
  beta <- append_col(beta1,beta2);

The copying's not so expensive relative to gradient
calcs, but no need to build up beta if you don't need
it.

And you probably want beta to be a local variable
rather than transformed parameter so that you don't
see it in the output (unless you're going to need it
in more than the block where it's defined).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the Eigen tutorial link.  That's very helpful.
I'm not surprised they didn't literally use a ragged
array structure --- in fact they implemented a ragged-like
structure the way I suggested in the v2.6 manual chapter
(and was previously buried in the LDA model description).

We'd eventually want to use Eigen.  We go with the
column major default for dense matrices now.  It looks
like they default to compressed column, which makes sense
for consistency, so I'd just go with that.  It does
make a difference in terms of how many other indices you
need to store, but neither dominates on all sparse matrices.

If you just implement a fully templated function, it'll
deal with all instantiations --- that's what the Stan functions
get compiled to.  Then you can specialize for the cases you
really care about and build specialized derivatives.

At the other extreme are our density functions, which use
a lot of template magic to vectorize, drop constant terms,
and work for first and higher order autodiff.  Everything
we do now needs to either take the templated route or also
implement forward mode.  We're about to knock that off so
that we can do MML, VB, EP, etc.

- Bob

P.S.  It seems like Google group's compressing losing all
indentation in replies.  Very annoying.   Did we mess up
a setting somewhere perhaps?

Be careful!  using absolute values is very dangerous
as it will typically lead to two posterior modes depending
on how l and b are constrained.  In your case, swapping
signs on l and b will lead to the same answer once you
apply fabs().

This could very likely be the cause of poor n_eff --- if
two chains land in different modes, R-hat and n_eff get very low because
they estimate means from all of the chains combined and
then make sure each chain matches the global mean.

The standard GLM solution if you want to constrain
a linear predictor to be positive is to exponentiate.

- Bob

Your c_one function needs to be templated to allow for an arbitrary scalar type. So:
1. prefix your function with 'template <typename T>'

3. Replace y(0,0).val() with y(0,0)

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
What do you mean by a "jumpy trace"?  If you're
using RStan, what does the pairs() plot look like?

Can it fit simulated data?  Often Poisson has a problem
because the underlying data is overdispersed (even though
you have a predictor mu here).  So it could just be
that the model doesn't fit the data well.

The model is also only weakly identified by priors (and
by pinning B[1] == 0).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Does anyone have suggestions on how to make these
messages clearer?  I'm taking a pass through errors now
and this particular one seems to confuse a lot of our
users.

The problem you're having is that you're passing an
array of vectors to to_matrix().  The only valid arguments
are either a matrix, a vector, a row vector, a 2D array
of real or a 2D array of int.  An array of vectors doesn't
match any of those.

For a start, I think I'll replace "vector[1]" with just
"vector[]".  That will at least make the type print out match
the way way types are defined in functions.  I think vector[1]
is confusing with the declaration.  So "int[2]" would look
like "int[,]".

messages.subject: Modelling categorized, overdispersed count data
messages.subject_clean: Modelling categorized, overdispersed count data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm interested in modelling a NB distribution based on overdispersed count data. No problem in itself, except that the count data are categorized (and aggregated) as follows:

  N  count_cat   unit
 y1          0      1
 y2        1-9      1
 y3      10-19      1
 y4        20+      1
 y5          0      2
 y6        1-9      2
 y7      10-19      2
 y8        20+      2

The first column holds the number of obserations of counts within a count category (second column, four categories with known bounds) for a certain hierarchical unit (third column). I want to quantify the underlying NB distribution in terms of mean and overdispersion (at some point in a hierarchical fashion, but not for now). My main question is how to efficiently model this in Stan (in terms of efficient sampling)? I can think of two general approaches:
Use the neg_binomial_2 functions:
Model the zero count category directly using increment_log_prob(y1 * neg_binomial_2_log(0, mu, phi))
Model non-zero count categories using increment_log_prob(y3 * log( neg_binomial_2_cdf(19) - neg_binomial_2_cdf(9) )), which may not be particularly stable (and expensive?) due to the cdf's and the logarithm, right? As a counterpart to the log_sum_exp function, a stable log_min_exp function would be nice here: increment_log_prob(y2 * log_min_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(9), neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0))).
Alternatively, use the categorical function, and find a smart way to directly translate the probability density function for a NB distribution to a categorical distribution for count data categories with known bounds. CAVEAT: not sure how stable and efficient the calculations would be. Insights / tips are welcome!

Thanks,

Luc

> On Feb 23, 2015, at 12:34 AM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear all,
>
> I'm interested in modelling a NB distribution based on overdispersed count data. No problem in itself, except that the count data are categorized (and aggregated) as follows:
>
>   N  count_cat   unit
>  y1          0      1
>  y2        1-9      1
>  y3      10-19      1
>  y4        20+      1
>  y5          0      2
>  y6        1-9      2
>  y7      10-19      2
>  y8        20+      2
>
> The first column holds the number of obserations of counts within a count category (second column, four categories with known bounds) for a certain hierarchical unit (third column).

It would be better to use the actual data if you have it,
but I'm going to assume this is all you have.

> I want to quantify the underlying NB distribution in terms of mean and overdispersion (at some point in a hierarchical fashion, but not for now). My main question is how to efficiently model this in Stan (in terms of efficient sampling)? I can think of two general approaches:
> 	• Use the neg_binomial_2 functions:
> 		• Model the zero count category directly using increment_log_prob(y1 * neg_binomial_2_log(0, mu, phi))

That's the best thing to do for zero counts.

> 		• Model non-zero count categories using increment_log_prob(y3 * log( neg_binomial_2_cdf(19) - neg_binomial_2_cdf(9) )), which may not be particularly stable (and expensive?) due to the cdf's and the logarithm, right?  ...

The negative binomials are pretty hairy computationally because
they call beta_cdfs, which in turn call various gamma and
digamma functions.  But you can always try it and see how stable it
is.  This seems like the cleanest approach in terms of being able
to easily read the program.

> 	• Alternatively, use the categorical function, and find a smart way to directly translate the probability density function for a NB distribution to a categorical distribution for count data categories with known bounds. CAVEAT: not sure how stable and efficient the calculations would be. Insights / tips are welcome!

For this case where you know the sizes are limited, it should be pretty
easy and stable to compute these directly.  You can use log_sum_exp
to get the log masses for the 1-9 and 10--19 cases, the 0 case is easy,
and you can use log_1m_exp() to get the remainder, and then do everything
on the logit scale so you can use categorical_logit.  Here's some pseudo code:

  counts <- c(y1,y2,y3,y4);

  lp1 <- nb2_log(0, ...);
  lp2 <- log_sum_exp({ nb2_log(1,...), ..., nb2_log(9, ...) });
  lp3 <- log_sum_exp({ nb2_log(10,...), ..., nb2_log(19, ...) });
  lp4 <- log1m_exp(log_sum_exp({ lp1, lp2, lp3 }));
  increment_log_prob(y1 * lp1);
  increment_log_prob(y2 * lp2);
  increment_log_prob(y3 * lp3);
  increment_log_prob(y4 * lp4);

No need to go through categorical() here.

The { ... } notation is meant to indicate array formation.
log1m_exp is another special function.

Not pretty, and it won't be efficient for large ranges, but
should be OK for the actual cases of 1, 1--9, 10--19, and 20+.

> As a counterpart to the log_sum_exp function, a stable log_min_exp function would be nice here: increment_log_prob(y2 * log_min_exp(neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(9), neg_binomial_2_cdf_log(0))).

Feel free to file a feature request.  I'd make it log_minus, though, because
"min" confused me at first thinking you meant minimum.

We really do need efficient versions of this for truncated densities.
Right now, we just do the naive thing in the generated code, taking
the log of the difference on the non-log scale.

- Bob

unless you are doing custom initialization and initialize
to NaN.

If you define a parameter with lower=0, the
sampler will operate on (-inf,inf) and use exp()
to transform to (0,inf).  exp() won't produce NaN
even if you give it infinite inputs (it'll return 0
or inf).

range checking, could it?  I thought that just led
to a NaN gradient if the value was NaN, not vice-versa.

It really really helps us debug if you send us the
full info on how you called Stan.  Which interface
did you use and what was the exact command you used
to invoke it?

Could you send us data?  In general, we advise simulating data
according to your model anyway to make sure the program can fit it.

messages.body_plain:
I still don't know why that particular error's coming up, but I
do see that the model's posterior is very difficult.

I managed to fit it with:

  fit <- stan("heckman_hete.stan",data=data_list,
              iter=4000,init=0,chains=2,
              control=list(adapt_gamma=0.99,stepsize=0.005));

Setting adapt_gamma=0.99 tells it to target a low step size (more
stable) in order to have a high acceptance rate and stepsize=0.005
tells it to start with a smallish step size.  In general, upping
the target acceptance rate (adapt_gamma) and dropping stepsize will
result in more stable iterations.

The problem is that the effective sample size per iteration is very very
low (on the order of 1/50 to 1/1000) and the posterior intervals are very
wide.  This can come from a truly hard problem or because the model is
not well identified.

In particular, the sigma_eq parameters take very wide excursions
up to values over 1000 on some chains.  A strong prior on this
would probably help tame the behavior --- the Cauchy is consistent
with extreme values.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 23, 2015, at 8:01 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Many thanks for the reply and the example - very clear!
>
> one question:
>
> Given I'm trying to fit a zero-intercept model, y ~ 0 + beta * x
>
> For the construction of the predictive distribution, does it make a (big) difference between
> 1. y_tilde <- normal(beta * x_tilde, sigma);
> 2. y_tilde <- beta * x_tilde, sigma

Whether there's an intercept or not doesn't matter.
Your (2) isn't well formed --- did you just mean
beta * x_tilde?

> Clarification on my original question inline:
> More below.
>
> > Here is the question:
> >
> > I used STAN to fit a 2-predictors, zero intercept linear model to my data and create a predictive posterior distribution using a new point data.
> >
> > Stan code as follow:
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=0> N; // num of obs
> >   vector[N] y;
> >   vector[N] ri;
> >   vector[N] rc;
> >   real c_new;
> > }
> > parameters {
> >   real<lower=0> beta_i;
> >   real<lower=0> beta_c;
> >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> > }
> > model {
> >   beta_i ~ normal (1, 2);
> >   beta_c ~ normal (1, 2.5);
> >
> >   y ~ normal (ri * beta_i + rc * beta_c, sigma);
> > }
> > generated quantities {
> >   real y_new;
> >
> >   // assume i_new to be 0
> >   y_new <- normal_rng (c_new * beta_c, sigma);
>
> This doesn't match your model because there's only one
> predictor, so I'm a bit confused about what you're trying to do.
>
>
> For the model, I'm trying to fit:
> y ~ ri + rc + 0
>
> For the predictive distribution, i have implicitly set ri = 0, hence I left it out in the generated quantities section. Should i had fully spec out ri to be 0 instead?

If you know the predictor's zero, you can drop the term.

> > }
> >
> > so far so good, using this, i seem to be able to get a posterior distribution based on a supplied value of c_new.
> >
> > Now, instead of using a single point forecast, c_new. I want to use a normal distribution centered at c_new with externally specified standard deviation.
>
> I don't understand why you'd want to do this.  You could
> make predictions for a bunch of new points, but why a normally
> distributed bunch of points?
>
>
> The idea behind this is as follow:
>
> 1. Let's forget ri for a second and assume the model to be fitted y ~ rc + 0

Only a subset of the Stan devs are familiar with the R expression
language.  I think this reduces to

 y[n] <- rc * x[n] + epsilon[n];
 epsilon[n] ~ normal(0,sigma);

or

  y[n] ~ normal(rc * x[n], sigma);

> 2. I have a  set of y and rc and want to predict y if given rc (predictive distribution with single point rc)

This is still a bit vague, but what I think you're saying is that
you have ourcomes

  y[1] ... y[N]

and predictos

  rc[1] ... rc[N]

and you want an intercept-only regression of y on rc.
Then you want to predict y[N+1] for a new rc[N+1], or
in Andrew's notation,  y_tilde[1] for a new rc_tilde[1].

So you want the predictive posterior:

  p(y[N+1] | rc[1:N], y[1:N], rc[N+1])

or again in Andrew's notation:

  p(y_tilde[1] | rc[1:N], y[1:N], rc_tilde[N+1])

> 3. But, I actually don't know rc, i only have an estimate rc, e_rc = rc + err.

You mean you have measurement error on your predictor?
That's a different problem.

> 4. For simplicity, I would model err as N(0, f_sd) - where f_sd would be estimated from another set of data

I'm lost as to what err and f_sd are.

> 5. So. the goal is the find the predictive distribution of y given data set (y, rc), new estimate: e_rc and historical error of estimate: f_sd.
>
> Perhaps, there is a much more efficient/elegant way to do this?

I'm still not sure I 100% understand what you're trying to do,
but if it's what I spelled out above, then the right way to do it
is the code I sent before.

And yes, you properly need the sd term.

- Bob

What does alpha in the traceplots correspond to in the
model?  If it's A, the prior is very misspecified
because the posterior is in the range of 10e6 and
the prior is normal(0,5).

That's also a very wide prior on elascticity, which
fits very close to 0.9 and gets a cauchy (0, 2.5) prior.
This is less worrying than the prior for A.

Otherwise, I don't really know enough about these models
and don't have enough time to dive in deeply.  I do know
that time series models can be hard to fit in terms of
n_eff per iteration, so I wouldn't worry too much about
the relatively poor mixing of elasticity.

If you repost to the list with a subject of the kind of
model you want help with rather than the current subject,
someone else may be able to help.

- Bob

> > >   vector[N] ri;

> > y ~ ri + rc + 0
> >
> > For the predictive distribution, i have implicitly set ri = 0, hence I left it out in the generated quantities section. Should i had fully spec out ri to be 0 instead?
>
> If you know the predictor's zero, you can drop the term.
>
> > > }
> > >
> > > so far so good, using this, i seem to be able to get a posterior distribution based on a supplied value of c_new.

> > > Now, instead of using a single point forecast, c_new. I want to use a normal distribution centered at c_new with externally specified standard deviation.

> and predictos
>

>

My actual application is in financial economics. But, in order to get away with many of the domain specific wordings/issues, let's consider this toy example:

My monthly electricity bill is my outcome: y[1] ... y[N]

Average temperature of the month is my predictor: avg_tmp[1] ... avg_tmp[N]

I use regression to relate the 2 in a linear model (side note: i live in Hong Kong, there is no heating. As temperature heats up, I use more air conditioning, thus driving up the bill. Let's assume usage is linear and unit cost and my behavior being constant (so, no intertemproral dynamics) for this example).

My goal is the predict my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1]

If i know avg_tmp_tilde[1], it would be straight forward.

But, i don't (and can't) know about it ahead of time.

Instead, let's assume that there is Bob who has made a point(type:real) forecast in each of the past N months in the past:

bob_tmp[1] ... bob_tmp[N]

and for the next month N+1:

bob_tmp_tilde[1]

For simplicity, let's assume Bob's (historical) forecast errors can be described/estimated as:
real bob_sd;
bob_err <- bob_tmp - avg_tmp
bob_err ~ normal (0, bob_sd);

Assume no inter-temporal dynamics, Bob's probabilistic forecast for avg_tmp_tilde[1] should be:

normal(bob_tmp_tilde[1], bob_sd)

Here, I want to know the prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Bob's forecast error history and Bob's forecast for month N+1:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1])

To add a bit more complexity to it.
Let's say Alice, another expert, has also made forecasts (independent of Bob's) in each of the past N months in the past and for the next month N+1:

alice_tmp[1] ... alice_tmp[N]
alice_tmp_tilde[1]

with similar error structure:
real alice_sd;
alice_err <- alice_tmp - avg_tmp
alice_err ~ normal (0, alice_sd);

Similarly, prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Alice's forecast error history and Alice's forecast for month N+1:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])

Assume that I have access only to forecasts made by Bob and Alice. So, my original goal of predicting my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1] should become:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])

Perhaps, similar problem has been covered in Andrew's book (I'm waiting for it to arrive at my bookstore) or elsewhere?

> > 4. For simplicity, I would model err as N(0, f_sd) - where f_sd would be estimated from another set of data
>
> I'm lost as to what err and f_sd are.
>
> > 5. So. the goal is the find the predictive distribution of y given data set (y, rc), new estimate: e_rc and historical error of estimate: f_sd.
> >
> > Perhaps, there is a much more efficient/elegant way to do this?
>
> I'm still not sure I 100% understand what you're trying to do,
> but if it's what I spelled out above, then the right way to do it
> is the code I sent before.
>
> And yes, you properly need the sd term.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
This is pretty straightforward predictive inference.
You just need to model avg_tmp and use that as the predictor.

Some more below.

> On Feb 24, 2015, at 4:43 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> ...

> My actual application is in financial economics. But, in order to get away with many of the domain specific wordings/issues, let's consider this toy example:
>
> My monthly electricity bill is my outcome: y[1] ... y[N]
>
> Average temperature of the month is my predictor: avg_tmp[1] ... avg_tmp[N]
>
> I use regression to relate the 2 in a linear model (side note: i live in Hong Kong, there is no heating. As temperature heats up, I use more air conditioning, thus driving up the bill. Let's assume usage is linear and unit cost and my behavior being constant (so, no intertemproral dynamics) for this example).
>
> My goal is the predict my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1]
>
> If i know avg_tmp_tilde[1], it would be straight forward.
>
> But, i don't (and can't) know about it ahead of time.
>
> Instead, let's assume that there is Bob who has made a point(type:real) forecast in each of the past N months in the past:
>
> bob_tmp[1] ... bob_tmp[N]

We try not to make point forecasts.  What we'll really have
is a density.  But that all gets handled behind the scenes
from Stan's point of view.  In Stan, it will look like a point,
but in the output it will be a set of samples approximating
a distribution.

> and for the next month N+1:
>
> bob_tmp_tilde[1]
>
> For simplicity, let's assume Bob's (historical) forecast errors can be described/estimated as:
> real bob_sd;
> bob_err <- bob_tmp - avg_tmp
> bob_err ~ normal (0, bob_sd);

I'd write this as

  bob_tmp ~ normal(avg_tmp, bob_sd);

But it'll give you the same answer either way.  The Gelman and Hill
regression book is great at relating all the notations for all
sorts of models (and even trying to deconstruct what people mean
by "random effect" and "fixed effect").

> Assume no inter-temporal dynamics, Bob's probabilistic forecast for avg_tmp_tilde[1] should be:
>
> normal(bob_tmp_tilde[1], bob_sd)

Right.

> Here, I want to know the prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Bob's forecast error history and Bob's forecast for month N+1:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1])

In Stan, the way to write this is this:

  y_tilde[1] <- normal_rng(alpha + beta * bob_tmp_tilde[1], y_sd);

This assumes a linear regression with slope and intercept on average
temperate, with y_sd being the error term.  Here, bob_tmp_tilde[1] will
be a parameter that's estimated.

If you only care about the posterior mean of y_tilde[1] and not
the uncertainty, then you can drop the normal_rng( , y_sd)
parts.

This is a good example of how Stan behaves as a probabilistic
programming language.

> To add a bit more complexity to it.
> Let's say Alice, another expert, has also made forecasts (independent of Bob's) in each of the past N months in the past and for the next month N+1:
>
> alice_tmp[1] ... alice_tmp[N]
> alice_tmp_tilde[1]
>
> with similar error structure:
> real alice_sd;
> alice_err <- alice_tmp - avg_tmp
> alice_err ~ normal (0, alice_sd);

This won't change anything if you just do the predictions
independently.  I'd suggest extending to a hierarchical model
that takes geo-spatial proximity into account.  I'm not 100%
sure how to do that without moving to Gaussian processes.

> Similarly, prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Alice's forecast error history and Alice's forecast for month N+1:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
>
> Assume that I have access only to forecasts made by Bob and Alice. So, my original goal of predicting my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1] should become:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
>
> Perhaps, similar problem has been covered in Andrew's book (I'm waiting for it to arrive at my bookstore) or elsewhere?

I'm not sure Gelman and Hill's regression book, or Gelman et al. Bayesian
Data Analysis book covers the case of uncertainty in prediction.  It
looks like a measurement error model, but it's not quite a measurement.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
[cc-ing stan-users]

Thanks.  We've known about some pending conflicts for
a while now.

The right thing to do from a programming point of view
is use namespaces.  R's defaults are very badly behaved
from a conventional programming point of view, because
they load all the namespaces into the top level.

I don't believe namespaces are widely known among R
programmers.  Hadley has a tutorial:

http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/namespace.html

In short, you should be able to use tidyr::extract for the
tidy version and rstan::extract for the Stan version.

- Bob

Otherwise, you might need to customize it a bit for your setup, but the code should be straightforward enough to follow and modify.
