messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Many thanks.

On Wednesday, February 25, 2015 at 6:43:18 AM UTC+8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This is pretty straightforward predictive inference.
> You just need to model avg_tmp and use that as the predictor.
>
> Some more below.
>
>
> > On Feb 24, 2015, at 4:43 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
> >
> > ...
>
> > My actual application is in financial economics. But, in order to get away with many of the domain specific wordings/issues, let's consider this toy example:
> >
> > My monthly electricity bill is my outcome: y[1] ... y[N]
> >
> > Average temperature of the month is my predictor: avg_tmp[1] ... avg_tmp[N]
> >
> > I use regression to relate the 2 in a linear model (side note: i live in Hong Kong, there is no heating. As temperature heats up, I use more air conditioning, thus driving up the bill. Let's assume usage is linear and unit cost and my behavior being constant (so, no intertemproral dynamics) for this example).
> >
> > My goal is the predict my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1]
> >
> > If i know avg_tmp_tilde[1], it would be straight forward.
> >
> > But, i don't (and can't) know about it ahead of time.
> >
> > Instead, let's assume that there is Bob who has made a point(type:real) forecast in each of the past N months in the past:
> >
> > bob_tmp[1] ... bob_tmp[N]
>
> We try not to make point forecasts.  What we'll really have
> is a density.  But that all gets handled behind the scenes
> from Stan's point of view.  In Stan, it will look like a point,
> but in the output it will be a set of samples approximating
> a distribution.
>
> > and for the next month N+1:
> >
> > bob_tmp_tilde[1]
> >
> > For simplicity, let's assume Bob's (historical) forecast errors can be described/estimated as:
> > real bob_sd;
> > bob_err <- bob_tmp - avg_tmp
> > bob_err ~ normal (0, bob_sd);
>
> I'd write this as
>
>   bob_tmp ~ normal(avg_tmp, bob_sd);
>
> But it'll give you the same answer either way.  The Gelman and Hill
> regression book is great at relating all the notations for all
> sorts of models (and even trying to deconstruct what people mean
> by "random effect" and "fixed effect").
>
> > Assume no inter-temporal dynamics, Bob's probabilistic forecast for avg_tmp_tilde[1] should be:
> >
> > normal(bob_tmp_tilde[1], bob_sd)
>
> Right.
>
> > Here, I want to know the prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Bob's forecast error history and Bob's forecast for month N+1:
> >
> > P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1])
>
> In Stan, the way to write this is this:
>
>   y_tilde[1] <- normal_rng(alpha + beta * bob_tmp_tilde[1], y_sd);
>
> This assumes a linear regression with slope and intercept on average
> temperate, with y_sd being the error term.  Here, bob_tmp_tilde[1] will
> be a parameter that's estimated.
>
> If you only care about the posterior mean of y_tilde[1] and not
> the uncertainty, then you can drop the normal_rng( , y_sd)
> parts.
>
>
> This is a good example of how Stan behaves as a probabilistic
> programming language.
>
> > To add a bit more complexity to it.
> > Let's say Alice, another expert, has also made forecasts (independent of Bob's) in each of the past N months in the past and for the next month N+1:
> >
> > alice_tmp[1] ... alice_tmp[N]
> > alice_tmp_tilde[1]
> >
> > with similar error structure:
> > real alice_sd;
> > alice_err <- alice_tmp - avg_tmp
> > alice_err ~ normal (0, alice_sd);
>
> This won't change anything if you just do the predictions
> independently.  I'd suggest extending to a hierarchical model
> that takes geo-spatial proximity into account.  I'm not 100%
> sure how to do that without moving to Gaussian processes.
>
> > Similarly, prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Alice's forecast error history and Alice's forecast for month N+1:
> >
> > P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
> >
> > Assume that I have access only to forecasts made by Bob and Alice. So, my original goal of predicting my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1] should become:
> >
> > P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
> >
> > Perhaps, similar problem has been covered in Andrew's book (I'm waiting for it to arrive at my bookstore) or elsewhere?
>
> I'm not sure Gelman and Hill's regression book, or Gelman et al. Bayesian
> Data Analysis book covers the case of uncertainty in prediction.  It
> looks like a measurement error model, but it's not quite a measurement.
>
> - Bob

Bob,

Many thanks.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Bob,

> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Do you have some recommandation for the hyperpriors ? Currently I'm using something like that :

bigmu ~ normal(5, 20);
bigsigma ~ gamma(.002,.001);
mu ~ lognormal(bigmu, bigsigma);

My mu[i] range from 100 to 300, the prior on bigmu largely covers this range.  And the prior on bigsigma largely covers the expected standard deviation of the posterior distributions of the mu[i].

Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :

> Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales

> so far away from standardized. llo Bob,

>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.
>
> Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:
>
> > mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)
>
> and then the prior is:
>
> > mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
>
> This requires the data to pull the posterior
> 3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
> are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
> unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
> more informative priors, not less informative ones.
>
> As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
> a pull to 200.
>
> I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
> simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
> R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
> looks fishy:
>
> > for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> > +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> > + }
>
> because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
> are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
> fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
> a negative binomial?
>
> This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:
>
> >    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> >    slope <- exp(logslope);
> >    for(j in 1:J) {
> >      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> >    }
>
>
> You're better off replacing the last line with:
>
>   sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;
>
> and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:
>
>   vector<lower=0>[J] mu;
>
> Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
> you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.
>
>   real<lower=0> slope;
>   real<lower=0> intercept;
>
> This would require reformulating the priors.
>
> You can also replace this:
>
> > for(j in 1:J){
> > +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> > +   }
>
>
> with the much more efficient
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advice about a model with mean dependent variance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] advice about a model with mean dependent variance
messages.body_plain:
Unlike lower-level priors, the hyperpriors have never seemed
very sensitive in anything I've done, so as long as you cover
the expected range, you should be OK.  The closer you can get
without being too restrictive, the better things will be
computationally.

I would stay away from those super-diffuse gammas --- there's
a discussion of priors in the manual chapter on regression (multiple
sections), and references to Andrew's papers on why not to use
the BUGS-standard (inverse) gamma distributions.

- Bob

> On Feb 25, 2015, at 8:09 PM, 'Stéphane Laurent' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hello Bob,
>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Do you have some recommandation for the hyperpriors ? Currently I'm using something like that :
>
> bigmu ~ normal(5, 20);
> bigsigma ~ gamma(.002,.001);
> mu ~ lognormal(bigmu, bigsigma);
>
> My mu[i] range from 100 to 300, the prior on bigmu largely covers this range.  And the prior on bigsigma largely covers the expected standard deviation of the posterior distributions of the mu[i].
>
>
>
>
> Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
> so far away from standardized. llo Bob,
>
>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.
>
> Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:
>
> > mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)
>
> and then the prior is:
>
> > mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
>
> This requires the data to pull the posterior
> 3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
> are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
> unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
> more informative priors, not less informative ones.
>
> As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
> a pull to 200.
>
> I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
> simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
> R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
> looks fishy:
>
> > for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> > +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> > + }
>
> because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
> are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
> fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
> a negative binomial?
>
> This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:
>
> >    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> >    slope <- exp(logslope);
> >    for(j in 1:J) {
> >      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> >    }
>
>
> You're better off replacing the last line with:
>
>   sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;
>
> and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:
>
>   vector<lower=0>[J] mu;
>
> Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
> you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.
>
>   real<lower=0> slope;
>   real<lower=0> intercept;
>
> This would require reformulating the priors.
>
> You can also replace this:
>
> > for(j in 1:J){
> > +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> > +   }
>
>
> with the much more efficient
>
>   mu ~ normal(200,30);
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Feb 18, 2015, at 10:24 PM, 'Stéphane Laurent' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> > I'm trying to fit a model given by J groups of observations, and the data within each group is generated according to a normal distribution with an unknown mean and  standard deviation is a linear function of the mean, with unknown slope and intercept.
> > I want to use "non-informative" priors for all parameters (below I use normal priors with large variance) and I get some problems.
> > The group means are positive and far from 0 (say >100), and the slope and intercept of the linear relation are constrained to be positive, therefore this guarantees a positive standard deviation.
> > Below is an example with simulated data. I observe the following issues:

messages.body_plain:
use rows() or cols().

> On Feb 26, 2015, at 12:12 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> Maybe I used the size call wrong, but the attached stan model does not compile for me. That is getting the size of a vector in a function does not seem to work.

size() is only defined for arrays.  And then
it's just the size of the first dimension.

The num_elements() function should work.  Or you
can use rows() or cols().

> BTW, functions are great, but I find myself writing stuff like the countPositives int the example in order to make simple declarations possible in the transformed data block like in the stan file. If a syntax like
>
> transformed data {
>   vector[sum(someInput>0)] vectorForPositiveStuff;
> }
>
> would be possible - that would be great!

The inefficient implementation that allocates a new array
and copies to it wouldn't be that hard to implement.  But
then we'd want to do it for all the operators, which means
a lot of cases.

> This may cause a headache for the language processing, but couldn't one possibly define this as lambda functions?

The C++ idiom to use to make it efficient would return an
expression template, which is like a lazy lambda function for
the whole value (someInput > 0).

Of course, if we introduced lambda functions into Stan, then
we could do these kinds of things very generally, with this
one being something like:

  sum(map(x.(x > 0), someInput))

x.(x > 0) would be a function that returned 1 if its input was > 0
and 0 otherwise.  map(function, container) would apply the function
elementwise to the members of the container, creating a new container.
Then sum() is what we already have.

What we really need is some way to test functions, though I
believe Jiqiang has workable solution for R.

- Bob

> On Feb 26, 2015, at 1:59 AM, Per Nielsen <evi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Rob and Bob

> Thank you both for your very fast answers!
>
> I will have a closer look at the transformed parameters block, and then I might as well use the "Matt trick" while I'm at it :)

The "Matt trick" is the non-centered parameterization if you
want to look it up in the literature.

> Btw, why isn't the "Matt trick" done internally in the rng? For me it seems like a pretty simple mapping.

Yes, it's the way the RNG works, but not how sampling works.

Sampling operates on the unconstrained parameter space, which
is defined by the constraints on the parameters --- each is mapped
to unconstrained support and the appropriate Jacobian adjustment
is applied to maintain the right sampling.  There's a chapter
detailing the exact transforms in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] rstan - how to use/re-use a stanfit object for different prediction
messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 26, 2015, at 2:03 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> ...

> The question is: what's the best/recommended way to do prediction with new values of x now I have a stanfit object?
>
> 1. I can added a generated quantities block into the STAN code, but that would require me to supply the new data at the same time with the fitting process - something not very clean from a design perspective (also practically, my system may not have all the new_data values available during the fitting phrase).

This is the cleanest way to do it.

>
> 2. Should I read off the mean and sd of the fitted parameters from stanfit object and then specify them in the data section of a different STAN code that does the sampling?

This will not give you full Bayesian inference.
It will use the posterior means as point estimates
and thus underestimate uncertainty in your estimates.

> 3. none of the above?

What you want to do is simulate one or more predictions
using an RNG for each draw in the posterior sample.
Then that gives you a sample for the predictions.

If you only care about the mean prediction, then you
can take the mean of this.  In some cases, this will work
out to the prediction you get using the posterior means
as point parameters in prediction.

> I guess the more generic version question is: what's the best way to "pass" estimated values from one STAN run (via stanfit object) to another STAN run?

If you really need to do this, the only option is to create
a Stan program that reads in the whole sample object and then
iterates through them generating predictions for each draw in
the sample.  Here's a super-duper simple case to illustrate:

data {
  int<lower=1> M;          // num posterior draws
  real mu[M];              // posterior draws for mu
  real<lower=0> sigma[M];  // posterior draws for sigma
}
model {
}
generated quantities {
  real y[M];
  for (m in 1:M)
    y[m] <- normal_rng(mu[m], sigma[m]);
}

You'll need to run it in the special fixed parameters mode or it'll
fail.

And of course, if you have predictors or other parameters, those
all need to be passed in the same way.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Working more and more with the Stan functions, I find them just wonderful to do all my computation work in my models. Now it would be even better if we could call these functions somehow from R.

Currently, I have to write a model for inference and one for simulation. With the Stan functions these two models look very much the same and doing the simulation would easily be doable from R if I could somehow call the Stan user functions defined in the model.

It looks to me that almost everything is there, i.e. the Rcpp glue between Stan and R is fairly thin and this should be doable.

Could this be done in Stan/rstan generally?
As an intermediate solution: Can I make some declarations manually in order to access the Stan user functions via Rcpp? Has someone experience in that or even has done it?

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to fit a variant of the CES function in Stan. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_elasticity_of_substitution

Q[i] = F (a K[i]^r +(1-a) L[i]^r)^(1/r)

where:
  r ∈ (-1,0)U(0,∞)
  a ∈ (0,1)
  F ∈ (0, <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity>∞)

And Q, K and L are >0 data.
 <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinity>

The parameter, r, has support over the union of the open continuous interval from -1 to 0, and the positive reals. There is, however, an undefined point at zero, which leads to a divergent gradiant warning when I initialize at zero. The model runs when initialized at different values, but I am wondering if the pole at zero leads to abnormal behavior in Stan more generally. Any ideas? Is there a way to define the constraints than <lower=-1>?

I think you will be okay as long as you don't initialize it to exactly zero. Or you could fill in the discontinuity at r = 0 with a Cobb-Douglas function. The derivative is smooth through zero so I think NUTS will be able to pass over it without experiencing the problems we sometimes see with abs() or piecewise functions.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
If you have prior knowledge about parameter r being positive or negative, I would use that to define the support (restrict to either positive or negative).

If you don't know this, you may consider defining two separate parameters real r_pos<lower=0> and real r_neg<lower=-1, upper=0>, calculate and temporarily store the log-posterior for each (using all the data), and then mix the two with to-be-estimated mixing weights real W_neg<lower=0,upper=1> and 1-W_neg. If you run into trouble because r_pos or r_neg is pulled towards zero, you can add some soft constraints using a prior with zero density at zero.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 28, 2015, at 6:10 AM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Sorry for answering my own question again; I clearly need to learn to take a little more time to try to solve things myself!
>
> Anyway, I now realize (thanks to reading http://www.paulbays.com/pdf/BayCatHus09.pdf), that the proper way to implement this mixture would be:
>
> model {
>     real lps_to_sum_exp[3] ;
>     real ps[2];
>     for( i in 1:trial_count ){
>         for( j in 1:3){

>             lps_to_sum_exp[j] <- von_mises_log(error[i],wrongLocs[i][j],10)
>         }

As of Stan 2.6, you can replace this:

>         ps[1] <- log(mix_proportion) + von_mises_log(error[i],pi,10)
>         ps[2] <- log1m(mix_proportion) + log_sum_exp(lps_to_sum_exp)
>         increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps))

with

  increment_log_prob(log_mix(mix_proportion,
                             von_mises_log(error[i],pi,10),
                             log_sum_exp(lps_to_sum_exp) ));

And just to be clear, this produces a mixture of top-level models like
your example, not a mixture at the element level, as is more traditional
in mixture modeling.  I'd think from your description you'd want to mix
at the element level, allowing varying memory among the subjects.

- Bob

>
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student
> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
>
> On Fri, Feb 27, 2015 at 2:53 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi folks,
>
> I'm trying to figure out how to code a specific kind of mixture model. To get to the model, let me first describe a couple data-collection scenarios of increasing complexity:
>
> [1] I show you a colored square briefly, then ask you to indicate its color by clicking a spot on a circular RGB color wheel. If we do this many times, each time measuring the radians of error in your response, we'd build up a distribution of responses that should be centered on zero error with some spread on either side, in which case the concentration parameter of a Von Mises distribution would be useful to quantify the fidelity of memory.
>
> [2] Now, instead of a single square, I show you multiple squares, each of a different color. After a brief period, all the squares turn grey, and arrow appears pointing to one, and you're asked to indicate the color (on the color wheel as in [1]) of the pointed-to square. If you have perfect memory for the location-and-color combinations, then your responses should be distributed as in [1]. However, possibly your location-and-color combination memory is imperfect and on some proportion of trials you report the color from one of the other locations, but with the same fidelity with respect to that location's color as when reporting the color from the pointed-to location.
>
> I know that data from many repetitions of scenario [2] should form a mixture of a Von Mises and ... something, but I'm not sure how to formulate the second mixture component. Any suggestions?
>
> To make things more concrete, if there were 4 locations on every presentation trial, I imagine that I should be supplying the following as data
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> trial_count ;
> real<lower=0,upper=2*pi()> error[trial_count] ;
>         vector<lower=0,upper=2*pi()>[trial_count] wrongLocs[3] ;
> }
>
> where "error" contains the trial-by-trial radians of error (centered on pi; pi==0 radians of error) relative to the pointed-to-location, and "wrongLocs" conatains the trial-by-trial locations on the color wheel of the other 3 colors, again relative to the pointed-to-location. Fixing the fidelity (Von Mises concentration) parameter at 10 for simplicity, we might then have
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=1> mix_proportion ;
> }
> model {
>     real lps_to_sum[4] ;
>     for( i in 1:trial_count ){
>        ps[1] <- log(mix_proportion) + von_mises_log(error[i],pi,10)
>        ps[2] <- log1m(mix_proportion) +???
>        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps))
>     }
> }
>
> So I'm trying to figure out what should replace the "???". Would it make sense for it to simply be:
>
> ps[2] <- log1m(mix_proportion) + ( von_mises_log(error[i], wrongLocs[i][1],10) + von_mises_log(error[i], wrongLocs[i][2],10) + von_mises_log(error[i], wrongLocs[i][3],10) )
>
> ?
>
>
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
If you want to sample from a uniform discrete distribution from 1 to N,
I'd suggest:

y <-  categorical_rng(rep_vector(0,N) / N);

Then if you need to move to a different starting point, just add an integer.

If you'd like to file a feature request for a discrete uniform RNG,
it wouldn't be hard to add.  We could also add the pmf and cdfs for
consistency, though these aren't very useful anywhere in a Stan program
other than to add normalizing constants, because we don't have integer
parameters.  We're pretty backed up at the moment, though.

- Bob

> On Feb 28, 2015, at 2:25 PM, Cody Ross <ctr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
> Thanks for that method of making the discrete uniform. I trying to do something less elegant with floor_int(uniform_rng(A,B+1)) that was probably a lot slower.
>
> The discrete uniform dist is not urgent, but is there any reason to keep the gradient destroying functions typed to reals in the gen. quant. block?

The ones that return reals also destroy gradients, so there's
really no reason not to include integer based versions other than
that we don't want to mislead users into doing things that cause
problems.  (They'd be an "attractive nuisance" in American legal
terms (not to imply our users are children!).)

We have the information in the parser to easily do this,
but the biggest downside is user-facing complexity in
the doc, which will probably lead to confusion, though restricting
the _rng functions hasn't seemed to have been a problem.

- Bob
